statement: As a result, applicants will be forced to have their cases reheard, burdening them further, financially and emotionally as well.
criterion: The enacted Act's transitional provisions and subsequent High Court customary marine title proceedings: true if applicants whose cases were already heard or decided under the previous test are required to have them reheard or redetermined; false if the amendments apply only prospectively to undetermined applications and no rehearing is required.
reasoning: The criterion's true-condition is met and its false-condition is squarely contradicted. The Amendment Act (Royal assent 24 Oct 2025) applies retrospectively to 25 July 2024: CMT orders granted between that date and enactment have no legal effect and must be reheard under the new, more restrictive test. Four already-granted awards of customary marine title covering approximately 341 km of coastline were overturned, with up to seven cases requiring rehearing. The Government approved $15 million toward affected applicants' rehearing costs, an implicit official concession of the financial burden Andersen described. The prediction has also already been borne out in practice: the Ruapuke Island Group was reheard and on 26 February 2026 Justice Churchman found they met the revised test, reaching the same outcome as the earlier August 2025 decision, i.e. they relitigated the case to arrive where they already were. Checked for the disconfirming possibility that the retrospective provision was dropped before enactment or that the Act applies only prospectively; multiple post-enactment sources and an actual completed rehearing rule that out. Caveat on sourcing: legislation.govt.nz returned HTTP 403, so the enacted text was confirmed via a law-firm analysis of the Act plus reporting of a rehearing conducted under the new test rather than from the statute directly.

statement: There is a reference in there to the prohibited grounds of discrimination under the Human Rights Act as a guiding light, but not the sole basis for refusing a petition, and this will be in place for six months, I suspect, that it will be seen as a useful innovation, and I hope will become a permanent feature of our Standing Orders, but that's not for today.
criterion: The Standing Orders of the House of Representatives as adopted at the next full Standing Orders review following the trial; true if a permanent Standing Order empowering the Clerk to refuse to host electronic petitions with highly discriminatory content is adopted, false if the sessional order lapses or is not carried into the Standing Orders.
reasoning: The sessional order Webb describes is confirmed: Parliament's published 'Sessional orders (54th Parliament) as at 17 December 2025' contains, under NON-LEGISLATIVE PROCEDURES, 'Electronic petitions with highly discriminatory content' — the Clerk may refuse to host an electronic petition if satisfied the content is highly discriminatory, must take account of whether it is threatening/abusive/insulting to a group by reason of a prohibited ground of discrimination under the Human Rights Act 1993, and must consult the Petitions Committee; Standing Orders 371, 372, 378 — 9 October 2025; Rule 4: 'This sessional order expires 6 months after the date on which it is adopted.' So the 'in place for six months' element of his statement is accurate, and the trial ran to roughly 9 April 2026. The criterion, however, tests the Standing Orders 'as adopted at the next full Standing Orders review following the trial'. That review — the Review of Standing Orders 2026, chaired by the Speaker — was still at the submissions/hearings stage in late 2025 (submissions from the Law Society, NZ Council for Civil Liberties, NZCCSS and the PCE all dated Sept 2025; first public hearing late Oct 2025), and I could find no Standing Orders Committee report presented and no new Standing Orders adopted as of 15 August 2026. Checking for disconfirmation, I also looked for evidence the order had been renewed, extended or replaced, or that the review had rejected it — none found either way; the most recent sessional-orders compilation published is the 17 December 2025 one. Resolve-by is 31 December 2026, so the naming event has not yet occurred. Not a failing grade — simply undetermined.

statement: Yes, it is correct: we have heard that there are going to be changes in funding through Te Māngai Pāho for shows such as Te Karere and also Marae, maybe even The Hui, but this little $6 million that might be generated out of advertising on our Christmas Day, on Anzac Day, on Easter, and our regular Sunday viewing, is not going to fix the fundamentals.
criterion: Te Māngai Pāho funding decisions and TVNZ/Whakaata Māori commissioning announcements for the 2026 funding round; true if funding for Te Karere and/or Marae was reduced, withdrawn or restructured, false if the programmes were funded on unchanged terms.
reasoning: The criterion is satisfied on the Te Karere limb, which alone meets the 'and/or' test. Te Māngai Pāho announced its news and current affairs funding round on 27 October 2025, about two and a half weeks after Lyndon spoke on 9 October 2025. Te Karere's TMP funding fell from $2.7 million to $1 million. The Hui received no TMP allocation at all (it had previously had $1m from TMP plus $788,000 from NZ On Air) and is cutting from 40 episodes to 26. The round as a whole was restructured: $11 million total, weighted toward regional news services, with $1.5 million to Whakaata Māori to establish a National News Hub, against a TMP baseline dropping from $66m to about $50m. On the disconfirming side, Marae was in fact funded — Marae 2026, 35 x 29 minutes, Pango Productions for TVNZ, up to $1,500,000 — so her naming of Marae did not come true as a cut, though it sat inside a restructured round. Her framing was appropriately hedged ('shows such as', 'maybe even The Hui'), and the direction and the naming of the affected programmes were right, with The Hui hit harder than she suggested. The criterion asked whether Te Karere and/or Marae was reduced, withdrawn or restructured; Te Karere was reduced by roughly 63 percent.

statement: If this bill passes, they will not be taking advantage of advertising and will not conduct any advertising or seek any advertising revenue with this repeal.
criterion: Radio Rhema's broadcast output on the days the bill deregulates (Sunday mornings, Good Friday, Easter Sunday, Christmas Day, Anzac Day morning) in the first full year after commencement; true if no advertising is carried on those days, false if advertising is broadcast.
reasoning: The Broadcasting (Repeal of Advertising Restrictions) Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 55) passed its third reading 93-29 on 14 October 2025, received Royal assent on 16 October 2025 and came into force the day after, 17 October 2025, repealing s 81 of the Broadcasting Act 1989 (which had restricted TV advertising on Sunday and Anzac Day mornings 6am-noon, and both TV and radio advertising on Christmas Day, Good Friday and Easter Sunday). The criterion specifies Radio Rhema's output across the deregulated days 'in the first full year after commencement', a window that closes around 17 October 2026, and sets a resolve-by of 26 December 2026 — both still in the future as of 15 August 2026. Some of the window has elapsed (Christmas Day 2025, Good Friday and Easter Sunday 2026, Anzac Day morning 2026, and Sunday mornings), and I found no report of Rhema carrying advertising on those days, but that is absence of evidence rather than verification: station airchecks and hour-by-hour ad logs are not public. Searching on the subject rather than the direction, the only source I could find asserting Rhema will not advertise is Marcroft's own statement in the third reading debate, which is circular. Countervailing context worth carrying forward: Rhema Media does sell airtime — it operates a dedicated advertising/sponsorship offering and describes a non-profit model of about five minutes of sponsorship per hour funded mainly by ~26,000 member subscriptions and donations — so the claim is specifically about the deregulated days, not about Rhema running no commercial content at all. Flagging that even at maturity this may resolve as uncheckable without broadcast monitoring.

statement: They’ve done that recently and they won’t be doing it for a long time to come, I imagine, but you never know, they might, and that is the system that we have, and we’re accountable for that.
criterion: The official Electoral Commission result of the next New Zealand general election (due by late 2026). True if the National-led Government is returned to office after that election; false if a change of government follows it.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on the official result of the next NZ general election. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon announced the 2026 general election for Saturday 7 November 2026. Today is 15 August 2026, so the election has not been held and no Electoral Commission result exists. Mid-August 2026 coverage describes an active campaign with polling still in flux (Taxpayers' Union-Curia and Roy Morgan both reporting a narrow coalition position, TOP near the 5% threshold), i.e. the outcome is genuinely open. Note: an automated summary of the Wikipedia article initially reported that National had been returned with 49 seats; that is a misreading of the article's incumbent/outgoing-government infobox, and is contradicted by every dated source, which treats the November vote as forthcoming. No result to judge against yet.

statement: Much money has been spent and the predictions are that we have another 20 or 30 years of litigation, and so there are many elements of this legislation that need further work.
criterion: High Court and Ministry of Justice records of undetermined Takutai Moana applications. True if customary marine title applications or appeals under the Act remain before the courts in 2045; false if all applications have been finally determined or the pathway has been closed by then.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether customary marine title applications or appeals under the Takutai Moana Act remain before the courts in 2045; the resolve-by date is 2045-12-31, nineteen years away. Nothing observable now can settle it. For context only (not a resolution): the pathway is plainly still active in 2026 — the High Court's Takutai Moana list continues to produce judgments (e.g. Re Ngai Tumapuhia-a-Rangi Hapu Inc (No 3) [2026] NZHC 1365, 22 May 2026; the Ruapuke rehearing, 26 February 2026), and the 2025 Amendment Act's retrospective transitional provisions forced re-hearings of orders made from 25 July 2024, which adds litigation rather than closing it. That is consistent with the direction of the claim but does not test a 2045 endpoint.

statement: My friend and colleague Arena Williams just went through a particular claim that has been decided but will have to be relitigated, which raises the transitional provisions.
criterion: Court records for the Ruapuke Island customary marine title application after enactment: true if the application must be reheard or redetermined under the amended test, false if the existing High Court order stands undisturbed (including if the Bill is amended to carve it out or does not pass).
reasoning: The criterion is true if the Ruapuke Island application had to be reheard or redetermined under the amended test, and false only if the existing High Court order stood undisturbed (including if the Bill were carved out or failed). The Bill passed: the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Act 2025 had its third reading on 21 October 2025 and received Royal assent on 24 October 2025, applying retrospectively from 25 July 2024 so that customary marine title orders granted in that window have no legal effect and must be reheard under the new, more restrictive test. The Ruapuke Island Group's title was granted by the High Court in August 2025 — squarely inside that window — and the application was in fact reheard: Justice Churchman delivered judgment on 26 February 2026 after reconsidering all the evidence under the amended law, reaching the same outcome (continuous holding in accordance with tikanga since 1840, exclusive use and occupation without substantial interruption). Ngai Tahu criticised the rehearing as an unfair burden re-imposed on the whanau. Checked for the disconfirming reading — that the order simply stood — and it does not hold: the earlier order was displaced and a fresh determination was required. The unchanged result does not bear on the criterion, which is about relitigation, not outcome.

statement: All of these groups, as well as other whānau, who have very important rights will have their judgments null and void, so they will not be entitled to any compensation for the loss of time, for the loss of opportunity, and for the sweat and tears that they have put into their hearings.
criterion: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Act as enacted, plus any accompanying appropriation or ex gratia scheme. True if the enacted Act sets aside or requires redetermination of existing CMT judgments AND provides no compensation or costs recovery to affected applicant groups; false if existing judgments are preserved, or if any compensation, costs or ex gratia payment mechanism for those applicants is established.
reasoning: The Act (Royal assent 24 Oct 2025) does what she predicted on the judgments limb: Schedule 1AA deprives of legal effect CMT decisions, agreements and orders made between the 25 July 2024 policy announcement and enactment, requiring seven cases to be reheard under the tightened s58/s59 test — four of them cases where CMT had already been recognised (the High Court reheard evidence under the amended law, with Churchman J issuing redeterminations in Feb 2026). Two things defeat the criterion as written, though. First, judgments finally decided before the July 2024 announcement were preserved, so it is not 'all of these groups'. Second, the criterion makes it false if 'any compensation, costs or ex gratia payment mechanism for those applicants is established', and one was: Cabinet approved up to $15 million, held as a tagged contingency (Treasury supported the contingency approach), to contribute to the rehearing costs of affected applicants — on top of the pre-existing Takutai Moana Financial Assistance Scheme Court Workstream. That $15m is a contribution to rehearing costs, not compensation for the lost time, lost opportunity or prior effort she specifically named, so her underlying grievance is not answered; but a costs mechanism plainly exists, so the prediction is materially overstated rather than borne out.

statement: So the anticipation is that there would be a lot more movement of federation polytechnics than there would be of anchor polytechnics.
criterion: New Zealand Gazette notices and Orders in Council recording polytechnic designation changes under the new Part 4 regime between commencement and 31 December 2030; true if more federation polytechnics enter or leave federation status than institutions gain or lose anchor polytechnic status, false if anchor designation changes equal or exceed federation movements.
reasoning: The criterion's counting window runs from commencement (1 January 2026) to 31 December 2030; it is currently August 2026, so under four years of the window has elapsed and the comparison cannot be settled. Interim state of the ledger, for what it is worth, runs in the direction she predicted: the Open Polytechnic was designated anchor polytechnic of the Federation at establishment and no anchor designation has changed since, while federation-side movement is already underway — NorthTec, WITT and a merged Whitireia/WelTec are to be established by Orders in Council as stand-alone Federation members from 1 January 2027, and Tai Poutini Polytechnic transfers its operations into the Open Polytechnic on the same date. That is at least three federation-status entries pending against zero anchor changes, but the Orders in Council had not been made at time of checking and the window has four more years to run.

statement: I’m hoping that they will be able to grow that again, and I consider that we are not going to be faced with the sort of question of additional $930 million – odd being needed over the following nine years.
criterion: Vote Tertiary Education Budget documents and TEC/Ministry of Education funding bids for the vocational education sector through to 2034; false if a bid or appropriation of approximately $900m or more (beyond existing baselines) for the polytechnic network arises in that period, true if no such request materialises.
reasoning: The claim covers the nine years following 2025 and the criterion runs to 31 December 2034; only the first of those years has passed, so a bid could still arise at any point in the remaining eight. Nothing approaching the ~$900m threshold has appeared so far: the ten re-established polytechnics were capitalised with about $325m carried over from Te Pukenga's reserves at establishment rather than a new appropriation, and Budget 2026's vocational spending is at a much smaller scale — two years of transition support for the ITPs, $87m for Youth Guarantee places, $69m for Trades Academy places, plus targeted sums such as $2m for the Open Polytechnic's takeover of Tai Poutini and $3.6m for NorthTec via the Strategically Important Provision Fund, with tertiary subsidy rates frozen. Officials have publicly warned (July 2026) that some polytechnics remain financially at risk, so the possibility of a later large bid is live rather than closed off.

statement: In the past they have formed statutes and they have been different for each institution, and I would expect that, again, they will be different, so they won’t exclude any of the representation from staff or from students or from iwi.
criterion: The council statutes/constitutions adopted by the new ITP councils after establishment: true if none of them excludes staff, student or iwi representation from the non-ministerial seats; false if one or more adopted statutes makes no provision for one of those groups.
reasoning: The criterion tests statutes/constitutions adopted by the new ITP councils after establishment. The ten polytechnics were established by Orders in Council in force 25 Nov 2025 and began operating 1 Jan 2026, but each council was seated with only three or four ministerial appointees; the non-ministerial seats the claim concerns are still being filled (Ara: four members as at its 24 Feb 2026 meeting, recruitment for the remaining three underway, 'Council Member Appointment Process' still on the agenda; Otago Polytechnic: four confirmed, three more to come). The Minister's Dec 2025 appointments release refers to 'their individual constitutions' but none has been published, and I found no adopted statute for any of the ten specifying whether staff, student or iwi representation is provided for. Nothing to test yet; resolve-by is 30 June 2027.

statement: It will see courses cancelled in the further-out parts of Northland: Kaikohe, Kaitāia, marae-based programmes.
criterion: NorthTec's published programme and campus offerings for Kaikohe, Kaitāia and its marae-based programmes, compared against its 2025 offerings, plus any TEC/NorthTec announcements of course discontinuation. True if courses at those sites or the marae-based programmes are cancelled; false if delivery at those sites continues at comparable breadth.
reasoning: NorthTec does not become a stand-alone polytechnic until 1 Jan 2027 and the Mid North property decision (Kerikeri vs Ngāwhā, leased from Far North Holdings) was still open, so the comparison window the criterion sets runs into 2027. On present evidence delivery continues at both named sites: NorthTec's current programme listings show 7 programmes at Kaitāia and 8 at Ngāwhā (the campus near Kaikohe), including Puawānanga Tapuhi Māori (Bachelor of Nursing Māori) and the Diploma in Whānau Ora, and the campuses page still lists Kaitaia, Ngāwhā and Whangārei. The documented cuts — 11 programmes in forestry, primary industries, apiculture, pest control and creative writing, plus ~58 FTE roles — were proposed in March 2025, before the statement, and were not attributed to those sites; the Kaitāia change was consolidation from leased Redan Rd into the owned Oxford St building, not cessation of delivery. No evidence found of marae-based programmes being cancelled; NorthTec still describes support for marae-based te reo delivery via Māori providers. A 2025 site-by-site baseline could not be retrieved (web.archive.org is not fetchable from this environment), which is a further reason not to resolve early. Evidence so far leans against the prediction rather than for it.

statement: Her timelines have ISBs to be established on 1 January 2026. That is not on track to be set up.
criterion: Whether industry skills boards were legally established and operating from 1 January 2026, per the commencement provisions of the enacted Act and TEC/Ministry announcements; the prediction is true if the establishment date slipped past 1 January 2026, false if the boards were established on that date.
reasoning: The establishment date did not slip. The Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Act 2025 passed 15 Oct 2025 and came into force 22 Oct 2025; the Cabinet paper of 24 Nov 2025 (proactively released Feb 2026) records that the eight Orders in Council establishing the ISBs were given a waiver of the 28-day rule so they came into force on 25 Nov 2025, expressly 'to enable the new polytechnics and Industry Skills Boards to be operational from 1 January 2026', with the six Workforce Development Council disestablishment orders taking effect 1 Jan 2026. The transition happened on schedule: Waihanga Ara Rau was disestablished 31 Dec 2025 and its functions passed to the Energy and Infrastructure, Construction and Specialist Trades, and Electrotechnology and IT ISBs; Careerforce transferred into the Education, Health and Community ISB as a business division on 1 Jan 2026; the ISBs have operating websites. I looked specifically for evidence of a delayed or partial establishment and found none.

statement: That is going to make a huge difference to those polytechnics and industry skills boards.
criterion: Annual reports of the recapitalised polytechnics and TEC monitoring reports for the first full financial year after the recapitalisation is paid. True if a majority of recipient polytechnics report a materially improved operating result (deficit substantially reduced or surplus restored) relative to the year before payment; false if their operating results are broadly flat or worse, or if further Crown support is required in that period.
reasoning: The criterion tests annual reports of the recapitalised polytechnics and TEC monitoring for the first full financial year AFTER the recapitalisation is paid. The ten regionally-governed polytechnics and eight Industry Skills Boards only began operating independently on 1 January 2026, funded with $325m transferred from Te Pukenga (work-based learning divisions recapitalised with $62.7m). Their first full financial year as independent entities is calendar 2026, whose annual reports and TEC monitoring are not published until mid-2027 — consistent with the resolve-by date of 2027-06-30, which has not passed. Interim signals only, not a verdict: the eleven institutes that left Te Pukenga told RNZ they were forecasting surpluses for 2026, while Te Pukenga itself budgeted a $16m deficit for its four remaining institutes; at the same time further targeted Crown money is already flowing (TEC SIP fund ~$10m indicative across 12 polytechnics in 2026, NorthTec $3.6m in 2026 and $2.75m in 2027, Open Polytechnic $2m for the Tai Poutini takeover plus $1m/yr 2028-31), which will bear on the criterion's 'further Crown support is required' clause when the reports land.

statement: We're now growing now; we're expected to grow even further in quarter four.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP (production measure, seasonally adjusted) for the December 2025 quarter, released March 2026: true if December-quarter growth is positive and larger than the September 2025 quarter; false if the December quarter is negative or lower than the preceding quarter.
reasoning: Stats NZ (released 19 March 2026): GDP rose 0.2 percent in the December 2025 quarter, following a 0.9 percent increase in the September 2025 quarter (the September quarter was first published at +1.1 percent in December 2025 and revised down to +0.9 percent in the December-quarter release). The criterion required December-quarter growth to be positive AND larger than the September 2025 quarter for 'true', and specified 'false if the December quarter is negative or lower than the preceding quarter'. 0.2 < 0.9, so the pre-registered false branch fires on either the original or the revised September figure. Checked for disconfirming evidence: the December quarter was positive, annual growth turned positive at +1.3 percent (first annual growth in more than two years), and the economy grew 1.1 percent across the second half of 2025 — so 'we're now growing' was accurate. But the specific prediction of growing 'even further in quarter four' was tested as acceleration, and Q4 decelerated sharply.

statement: On the question of hard hats and high-vis, I can assure you coal mining is about to improve those statistics.
criterion: Stats NZ HLFS/filled-jobs series for construction and mining employment over the four quarters following October 2025; true if construction and mining employment rises measurably, false if it is flat or continues to fall. Coal-sector employment (MBIE energy statistics) alone is roughly 1,000 FTE, so a materially visible move in the headline series is the test.
reasoning: The criterion names the HLFS/filled-jobs series for construction and mining over the four quarters following October 2025 — December 2025, March 2026, June 2026 and September 2026. The September 2026 quarter HLFS is not released until early November 2026 (resolve-by 2026-12-31 has not passed), so the series the criterion specifies is incomplete. What the three published quarters show, as interim signal rather than verdict: unemployment rose from 5.4 percent (March 2026) to 5.6 percent (June 2026), an 11-year high; seasonally adjusted goods-producing filled jobs (which contain construction and mining) were essentially flat — up 149 jobs in June 2026 and 602 in May 2026, with almost all net growth in services; construction employment remains about 8.4 percent (roughly 17,250 jobs) below its 2023 peak as at August 2026, with commentary describing construction as stabilised but not yet returned to growth; and mining/exploration is roughly 4,200 filled jobs (0.2 percent of employment) with forecast growth of only 0.3 percent a year to 2031. Counter-evidence checked: SEEK job advertisements for construction were up 35.1 percent year-on-year in June 2026, but vacancies are not the filled-jobs/HLFS series the criterion names. On the evidence so far there is no materially visible move in the headline series, but the fourth quarter is still outstanding.

statement: Exactly, Minister Collins: they will never get that chance.
criterion: The composition of the government formed after the next New Zealand general election: false if Labour, the Greens and/or Te Pāti Māori form or enter government; true if they do not.
reasoning: The criterion turns on the composition of the government formed after the next general election. That election is scheduled for Saturday 7 November 2026 (advance voting from 26 October); as of 15 August 2026 it has not been held, so no post-election government exists to assess. Resolve-by date 2027-01-31 has not passed.

statement: Again, all that we will see is our universities continuing to drop in some of those international rankings when it comes to how they’re perceived internationally.
criterion: The QS World University Rankings and Times Higher Education World University Rankings editions released after this statement, compared with the preceding edition; true if the majority of the eight New Zealand universities fall in position, false if the majority hold or improve.
reasoning: The criterion requires BOTH the QS and THE editions released after 15 Oct 2025. QS is in and supports the prediction: comparing QS 2027 (June 2026) with QS 2026, six of eight NZ universities fell — Auckland 65 to 67, Otago 197 to 198, Victoria Wellington 240 to 241, Waikato 281 to =293, Lincoln 407 to =419, AUT =410 to =431 — while only Massey (230 to 215) and Canterbury (261 to 257) improved. THE is not in: THE World University Rankings 2026 was published 9 October 2025, six days BEFORE the statement, so it is the preceding edition; the qualifying edition is WUR 2027, due at THE's World Academic Summit in autumn 2026 and not yet released as of 15 Aug 2026. Since that edition falls inside the 2026-12-31 resolve window, the item is only half resolved. Re-check after the THE 2027 release; on QS alone the majority did fall.

statement: I am confident they will complete this work and that decisions will be able to be made about their establishment in the new year.
criterion: Ministry of Education / Tertiary Education Commission announcements and Cabinet decisions on the establishment of the polytechnics not among the initial ten; true if establishment decisions for all remaining polytechnics are announced during 2026, false if any remain undecided or are wound up rather than established.
reasoning: The timing half of the prediction held: on 31 March 2026 — 'in the new year' — Simmonds announced decisions covering every polytechnic still inside NZIST (the renamed Te Pukenga) after the initial ten went standalone on 1 January 2026, so none remain undecided. But the criterion also fails if any are wound up rather than established, and one was: Tai Poutini Polytechnic is not being re-established; its operations transfer to The Open Polytechnic of New Zealand, the federation anchor. NorthTec, WITT, and Whitireia and WelTec are to be established as stand-alone regional polytechnics from 1 January 2027, with NZIST ceasing to exist on 31 March 2027. Decisions announced during 2026 as predicted; establishment for all remaining polytechnics, not achieved.

statement: On the question of fisheries, the proposed mining, God willing, to proceed off the coast of Taranaki will have minimal impact on the strength or the vitality of fisheries.
criterion: If the operation proceeds: EPA/Fisheries New Zealand consent-condition monitoring and stock assessments for the South Taranaki Bight fisheries in the years following commencement. True if no statistically significant decline in stock abundance or catch in the affected area is attributed to the operation; false if monitoring or assessment attributes a measurable decline to it. If the mining does not proceed by the resolve-by date, the claim is unresolvable rather than false.
reasoning: The criterion is conditional on the operation proceeding and then being monitored under EPA/Fisheries NZ consent conditions. It has not proceeded. The fast-track expert panel issued a draft decision on 5 February 2026 declining consent for TTR's South Taranaki Bight iron sand project, citing credible risks to marine fauna (pygmy blue whales, kororā), sediment plume and noise. TTR then withdrew the application entirely on 19 February 2026, before the final decision (due 18 March 2026). No mining has commenced, no consent conditions exist, and therefore no post-commencement stock assessments or monitoring data exist to test the claim against. The resolve-by date of 2030-12-31 has not passed, so the item is not yet due; TTR has historically reapplied after rejections (2014, 2016, Supreme Court 2021), so a future consent before 2030 is not impossible. Absent that, the criterion's own escape clause applies: the claim becomes unresolvable rather than false. Nothing here counts against Jones — the prediction's antecedent simply failed.

statement: Whether it's a savings tax, whether it's a property tax, whether it's a death tax, New Zealanders can be guaranteed that, behind the scenes, that's what they're cooking up to take to the next election.
criterion: Published tax policies of Labour, the Green Party and Te Pati Maori at the next general election. True if their released platforms include new taxes of the kinds named (a savings/wealth tax, a property or capital tax, or an estate/inheritance tax); false if none of the three campaigns on any such new tax.
reasoning: The criterion is satisfied: released 2026 platforms of the three opposition parties include new taxes of every kind Brown named. PROPERTY/CAPITAL TAX: Labour announced (Feb 2026) a flagship 28% capital gains tax on profits from residential and commercial investment property, effective 1 July 2027, with revenue ring-fenced for free GP visits. SAVINGS/WEALTH TAX: the Greens released (21 June 2026) a 2.5% annual 'super-rich tax' on net assets above $10m ($20m for couples), family home exempt, projected $3.8b in 2027/28; Te Pati Maori also campaigns on a wealth tax alongside a 48% top income rate. DEATH TAX: the Greens' capital acquisitions tax levies 33% on inheritances and gifts above $1m (family home, family farm and Maori land transfers exempt), projected $953m in its first full year. I checked for the disconfirming case — that none of the three would campaign on such a tax — and it does not hold; KPMG's and Deloitte's 2026 election tax trackers both group Labour, the Greens and Te Pati Maori as campaigning on structural tax reform including capital gains and wealth taxes. One qualification that does not change the verdict as written: the savings and death taxes are Green policy, not Labour's — Labour's CGT explicitly excludes KiwiSaver, shares, farms, businesses and inheritances. The criterion is framed across all three parties, so it resolves correct. Note the election (7 Nov 2026) has not yet been held, but the criterion turns on published platforms, which exist.

statement: We see New Zealand businesses getting a bit more confidence, and that will help them to employ more people.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / Quarterly Employment Survey: total filled jobs and employment level in the year following the statement. True if employment rises over that period; false if employment is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion's measurement window is the year following 2025-10-15, i.e. the September 2025 quarter to the September 2026 quarter. The September 2026 quarter HLFS/QES release is scheduled for early November 2026, after the 2026-10-15 resolve-by date, so the terminal data point does not yet exist. Interim data covering three of the four quarters: seasonally adjusted HLFS employment was 2,882,000 in the June 2025 quarter and was flat (0.0% change) in the September 2025 quarter, then 2,892,000 in the March 2026 quarter and 2,905,000 in the June 2026 quarter — roughly +23,000 (+0.8%) since the statement was made. So the direction is a rise, favouring the claim. But the two instruments the criterion names diverge in the latest quarter: HLFS employment rose 0.5% while QES filled jobs fell 0.4% and hours paid fell 0.3%. The disconfirming context is real too — unemployment rose to 5.6% in the June 2026 quarter, the highest since September 2015, with 171,000 unemployed, because labour force participation (70.7%) grew faster than jobs. Business confidence, the mechanism Collins invoked, has been volatile rather than steadily improving: ANZ's headline index ran 74 (Dec 2025) to 32.5 (Mar 2026) to 56.1 (Jul 2026), with employment intentions swinging from 22.3 in February to 9.4 in March to 18.1 in July. Recommend re-resolving after the November 2026 release.

statement: I do worry that the Government is opening itself up to potential legal challenges as a result of this inconsistency in drafting.
criterion: Court records and legal reporting on proceedings (e.g. judicial review) challenging decisions made under the Act's Order in Council provisions for anchor polytechnics, the federation, or industry skills boards; true if such a challenge is filed, false if none is by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The criterion resolves true if a judicial-review-style challenge is filed against decisions made under the Act's Order in Council provisions (anchor polytechnic, federation, industry skills boards) by 2028-10-15, and false only if none is by that date. As of 2026-08-15 no such proceeding was found: searches of NZ judicial review reporting, the Law Society courts roundup (May 2026), Employment Court 2026 appellate judgments, TEU news and Ministry/TEC releases surfaced none. The TEU's active 2026 High Court proceeding is against the amended Equal Pay Act 1972, not the VET reforms, and the Open Polytechnic anchor Order (SL 2025/300) shows no litigation attached. Disconfirming check: sector conflict is real (job cuts, union stop-work meetings, officials warning polytechs are at risk in July 2026), so litigation is plausible but unfiled so far. The window is open for another two years, so absence of a filing today cannot be scored false.

statement: Given the Government’s apparent unwillingness to invest in the new politics, the inevitable result will be fewer courses, fewer trainees, and fewer jobs in the system.
criterion: Tertiary Education Commission and polytechnic annual reports for 2026 and 2027 versus 2025 baselines; true if course offerings, trainee/apprentice enrolments and staff numbers across the ITP network all fall, false if enrolments and provision hold steady or rise.
reasoning: The criterion is explicitly pinned to TEC and polytechnic annual reports for 2026 and 2027 measured against 2025 baselines. As of 2026-08-15 the 2026 reporting year is not complete and no 2026 annual reports exist, so the named evidence cannot be consulted; the resolve-by date is 2027-12-31. Directional evidence so far leans toward the prediction — polytechnic enrolments fell 4.3% in 2025 (domestic down 5.1%), Te Pukenga shed 855 staff (~10% of workforce) after $80m+ funding cuts, Cabinet papers forecast roughly 1,000 jobs and 500 courses lost in the transition, and in July 2026 officials warned polytechnics remain at risk under the reforms. Disconfirming check: the 2026 work-based learning reforms are intended to expand industry-led training and international enrolments rose 5.4% in 2025, so the enrolment leg is not settled. The criterion requires courses, trainee/apprentice enrolments and staff numbers to ALL fall across the ITP network, which cannot be tested until the 2026 and 2027 reports are published.

statement: Well, the good news is that by the time that person leaves school, this Government will be history.
criterion: New Zealand general election results and subsequent government formation; true if the National-led coalition formed after the 2023 election is no longer the government of New Zealand at any point on or before 2030-12-31, false if it remains in office continuously through that date.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on general election results and government formation, true if the National-led coalition formed after the 2023 election ceases to be the government at any point on or before 2030-12-31. As of 2026-08-15 the next general election has been set for 7 November 2026 and has not been held; the Sixth National Government (National/ACT/NZ First) remains in office. No election result or change of government exists to check yet, and the resolve-by date is more than four years away.

statement: We have a projection for the next two years that we’ll grow faster than Australia.
criterion: Stats NZ and ABS annual real GDP growth for calendar 2026 and 2027; true if New Zealand's growth exceeds Australia's over that period taken together, false if Australia's is equal or higher.
reasoning: The criterion requires Stats NZ and ABS annual real GDP growth for calendar 2026 AND 2027 taken together; as of August 2026, calendar 2026 is incomplete and 2027 has not begun, so the evidence the criterion names does not yet exist. Partial data is mixed rather than decisive: ABS recorded 2.6% annual growth to the December 2025 quarter (fastest in nearly three years) but only +0.3% q/q in Q1 2026, slowing from +0.9% in Q4 2025. NZ forecasts for 2026 range from Westpac 2.0% (revised up from 1.5%), Treasury's Budget 2026 at 2.3% for 2026/27, HSBC 2.5%, down to OECD 1.4% (2026) and 2.2% (2027); IMF has Australia at ~2.0% for 2026. NZ is currently forecast to run ahead of Australia, but forecasts are not the criterion's evidence and outturns for both years are needed. Resolve-by is 2028-03-31.

statement: Well, that’s why I’d encourage the member to get in behind and support Fast-track, because there’s 25 renewable energy projects that will increase electricity generation in this country by 40 percent.
criterion: MBIE 'Energy in New Zealand' annual electricity generation statistics. True if total New Zealand electricity generation is at least 40 percent above its 2025 level once the fast-tracked renewable projects are commissioned; false if the increase is materially below 40 percent by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The criterion tests MBIE 'Energy in New Zealand' annual generation once the fast-tracked renewable projects are commissioned, with a resolve-by of 2032-12-31 — over six years away. No commissioning wave has occurred: MBIE's most recent quarterly data shows March 2026 quarter generation of 10,335 GWh, up only 1.9% (193 GWh) on the March 2025 quarter, against a 2024 annual baseline of 43,879 GWh. No MBIE annual edition beyond 2025 yet exists to measure against. Noted for future resolution (not scored now): the government's own fast-track announcement described 22 renewable electricity projects totalling ~3 GW that would lift generation CAPACITY by 'almost 30 percent', not 25 projects lifting GENERATION by 40 percent, so the speaker's framing already diverges from the official figures; but the criterion as written turns on commissioned generation, which remains open.

statement: The industry has earned $513 million in 2024 and is projected to surpass $750 million this year.
criterion: NZ Game Developers Association annual industry survey covering the 2025/26 year; true if reported sector revenue exceeds $750 million, false if it falls below.
reasoning: The $750m threshold is cleared on every available measure. The NZGDA annual survey released 26 September 2025 (a month before Upston spoke) reported pre-tax industry income of NZ$759.57m for FY2024/25, up 38.6% on $548m, with 1,418 FTEs and 95% ($709m) from international sales — so 'this year' as she meant it was already met. For the 2025/26 year the criterion names, NZGDA announced in June 2026 that the sector passed NZ$1 billion for the year ending March 2026 (two years ahead of its own target), and NZ On Air's 8 July 2026 GDSR release reports $829m combined studio revenue from rebate recipients alone in 2025/26, up 17% on $710m. NZGDA's final 2025/26 survey report is due September 2026, right at the resolve-by, but the margin over $750m is not close on either reading. Searched for disconfirming evidence (a downward revision or a lower NZGDA figure) and found none. One caveat that does not change the verdict: her $513m baseline comes from MBIE's GDSR Year Two Review (sales revenue at end-June 2024, LBD-based), while the $750m target is on the NZGDA survey measure, which put the comparable period at $548m — the pairing mixes methodologies and so overstates the implied growth rate, but the predicted figure itself was met.

statement: That name change would be at least clearer with people about what is happening here and what the effect of this will be: 13,000 of these dwellings around the country.
criterion: MBIE/Stats NZ building consent data for stand-alone dwellings consented under the new granny-flat exemption. True if roughly 13,000 (order-of-magnitude match) are consented nationally within ten years of the Act's commencement; false if the count is materially lower or higher over that period.
reasoning: The granny-flat consent exemption (Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Act 2025) only commenced 15 January 2026 — roughly seven months before this check. The 13,000 figure is itself the government/MBIE estimate of additional granny flats expected 'over the next decade', so the criterion's ten-year window runs to about 2036. No MBIE or Stats NZ data on dwellings consented/notified under the exemption has been published yet, so there is nothing to measure the order-of-magnitude match against. Not finding a count here reflects the horizon, not a failed prediction.

statement: The reality is that we have kids who have missed a hell of a lot of school. We’re two weeks away from NCEA exams. We’ve got 6,000 patients who are going to be disrupted, after Labour ran the wait-list up 30 times.
criterion: Health NZ / Te Whatu Ora reporting on procedures and appointments deferred because of the 23 October 2025 health strike; true if approximately 6,000 or more patients were affected, false if materially fewer.
reasoning: Health NZ chief executive Dr Dale Bramley estimated 6,000 patients would be impacted nationwide by the 23 October 2025 strike, comprising more than 900 elective admissions and ~1,300-1,380 first specialist appointments postponed plus other affected clinics. This reconciles the smaller figures reported elsewhere (RNZ carried Health NZ's '900+ procedures and 1380+ first specialist assessments', which is the planned-care subset only) with Luxon's number: he was quoting Health NZ's own nationwide estimate, not inflating it. I checked for disconfirming evidence — the widely circulated 4,300 figure belongs to a different (earlier nurses'/ASMS) strike, not 23 October. Caveat: this is Health NZ's pre-strike estimate; I found no post-strike actual tally published by Health NZ, and severe storms on 23 October independently disrupted services.

statement: Looking ahead, commodity export prices have levelled off, and so food inflation is expected to ease and inflation is expected to fall to somewhere near the mid-point target of 2 percent early next year, easing pressure on households and businesses.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation for the March 2026 quarter (published April 2026); true if the annual rate is at or near 2% (say 1.8–2.4%), false if it remains at or above roughly 2.7% or falls below 1.5%.
reasoning: Stats NZ reported annual CPI inflation of 3.1% in the 12 months to the March 2026 quarter (published April 2026), unchanged from the 3.1% recorded for the December 2025 quarter; consumer prices rose 0.9% in the March quarter alone. That is materially above the criterion's falsity threshold of roughly 2.7% and well above the ~2% midpoint Bishop predicted for 'early next year'. The largest upward contributor was electricity (+12.5%), followed by local authority rates (+8.8%) and meat and poultry (+8.6%), so the specific food-inflation easing he cited as the mechanism is not evident either. I checked whether a softer reading might hold — inflation neither eased toward 2% nor fell below the band; it simply held flat at 3.1%.

statement: The process will apply to all new claims made from 9 May 2025, and we expect that it will apply to around 100 claims a year.
criterion: Annual reporting by the redress agencies or the redress officer on the number of claims referred into the serious-offender process; true if the first full year's referrals are within roughly 50–150, false if they are materially outside that range.
reasoning: The Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill only passed its third reading on 25 June 2026, and the serious-offender process commenced 1 August 2026 — two weeks before the date of this check. The criterion requires annual reporting by the redress agencies or redress officer on the number of claims referred into the serious-offender process, covering a first full year. No such reporting exists yet and none could exist yet; searches for referral counts returned only legislative-framework material, no statistics. The resolve-by date (2027-06-30) has not passed.

statement: So, obviously, you're going to get an angry response from many of the victims out there.
criterion: Select committee submissions on the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill and public statements by survivor groups/advocates; true if a substantial body of survivor submissions and survivor-group statements oppose or criticise the bill's exclusion provisions, false if survivor submissions are largely supportive or negligible in number.
reasoning: The criterion is met on both limbs. Volume: the Social Services and Community Committee received 168 submissions from individuals and organisations, including 35 oral submissions from survivors, survivor advocacy groups and legal representatives — not negligible. Direction: the serious-offender exclusion was the single proposal that generated the most submitter feedback, and that feedback was critical — many submitters argued it ignored the link between abuse in care and later offending and diminished State responsibility. Willow-Jean Prime told the House that 92 percent of select committee submissions opposed the bill. Named survivors and advocates are on record objecting: Eugene Ryder ('I think it'll be very devastating'), Rawiri Waretini-Karena ('pulling the rug out from under them'), Cooper Legal's Lydia Oosterhoff (survivors 'punished twice'; the government 'is targeting people who the state in essence, largely created'). I checked for the disconfirming case — largely supportive or negligible survivor submissions — and found the opposite: even after passage in June 2026, survivor groups said the scheme still fell short of the Royal Commission's recommendations, which explicitly stated there should be 'no exclusion for serious offenders'. Note the claim is a low-specificity prediction ('an angry response from many'), so the bar is modest and it clears it comfortably.

statement: This sits alongside the Government’s pilot boot camp legislation, to put these into law—no doubt soon—to be again considered in this House.
criterion: The New Zealand Parliament bills register for the Government bill establishing military-style academies / boot camps for young offenders: true if it has its remaining stages and receives royal assent by the resolve-by date, false if it is still before the House, withdrawn, or defeated at that date.
reasoning: The Government bill establishing military-style academies for young offenders is the Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Bill (99-1, introduced 18 November 2024). It passed its first reading 21 November 2024 (68-49) and was referred to the Social Services and Community Committee, which was originally due to report back 20 May 2025. It did not complete its remaining stages by the resolve-by date of 2026-06-30: Wikipedia's boot camps article records that as at 6 March 2026 the bill 'was still progressing through its select committee stage at Parliament'; a bill tracker synced 31 May 2026 lists second reading, third reading and royal assent all as pending; and Oranga Tamariki's own current Military-Style Academies page still says the bill 'is progressing through the parliamentary process' and that details of future academies therefore cannot be confirmed. RNZ reported in December 2025 that passing the legislation 'may take another six months', and Oranga Tamariki ran its March 2026 academy as a further voluntary programme precisely because the sentencing power was not yet law. I searched specifically for passage/third reading/royal assent in 2026 and found no report of any — the disconfirming evidence is absent while multiple independent sources place the bill still before the House. The criterion's explicit false condition ('still before the House') is met. The prediction's hedge was 'no doubt soon'; more than eight months on, it has still not become law.

statement: It's the worst kind of rubbish that has come before this House, and it will be undone by a future Government, and we will have to stand up and apologise, Minister, for this nasty piece of legislation to somehow try and restore the honour of the Crown that you are disdaining.
criterion: New Zealand statute record: whether the burden-of-proof amendment to s 106 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 made by this bill is repealed or reversed by a subsequent Parliament, and whether a Crown apology is issued in respect of it. True if the provision is repealed or reversed; false if it remains in force in substantially its enacted form.
reasoning: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Act 2025 received royal assent 24 Oct 2025 and is still current legislation; the amended s 106 exclusive-use-and-occupation/burden-of-proof provision remains in force and is being applied by the High Court (e.g. the Feb 2026 Ruapuke rehearing decided under the revised tests). No subsequent Parliament has existed — the next general election is 7 Nov 2026 — so no repeal or reversal could have occurred, and no Crown apology has been issued. Labour, the Greens and Te Pati Maori publicly vowed on 22 Oct 2025 to repeal the law if they form the next government, which is a precondition for the prediction but does not resolve it. Criterion resolve-by date is 2032-12-31.

statement: When we get rid of this one-term Government, we’ll repeal this legislation back to 2003—2003.
criterion: The official Electoral Commission result of the 2026 New Zealand general election and the government formed after it: true if the National-led coalition (National, ACT, NZ First) does not form the next government; false if that coalition is returned to office.
reasoning: The criterion turns on the official Electoral Commission result of the 2026 general election and the government formed after it. That election is scheduled for Saturday 7 November 2026 and has not been held (current date 15 August 2026). The National/ACT/NZ First coalition under Christopher Luxon remains in office, so there is no result to test the criterion against. Checked for any early/snap election or date change and found none — Elections NZ and the Beehive both give 7 November 2026.

statement: This bill will not bring certainty; it will bring more litigation.
criterion: Count of Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act proceedings filed or reheard in the High Court and Court of Appeal in the two years after enactment, compared with the two years before: true if the volume rises; false if it falls or is flat.
reasoning: The criterion requires comparing MACA proceedings filed or reheard in the High Court and Court of Appeal in the two years after enactment (24 Oct 2025 - 24 Oct 2027) against the two years before; only about a third of the post-enactment window has elapsed and no such count is yet compilable. Interim evidence is directionally consistent with the prediction: the Act forced rehearings of seven cases, including four where customary marine title had already been recognised, with $15m of Crown funding approved for affected applicants' rehearing costs, and the first of those rehearing judgments (Ruapuke Island Group, Justice Churchman) was delivered 26 February 2026. But statutorily mandated rehearings are not the same measure as the filing-volume comparison the criterion specifies, and the window closes 2027. Criterion resolve-by is 2027-12-31.

statement: Your reign as Government is for one more year, so don't get too comfortable.
criterion: The result of the 2026 New Zealand general election and the government formed after it: true if the National-led coalition does not form the next government; false if it is returned to office.
reasoning: The 2026 NZ general election is scheduled for Saturday 7 November 2026 and has not yet been held (today is 2026-08-15). No post-election government has been formed, so the criterion — whether the National-led coalition returns to office — cannot be assessed. Resolve-by 2026-12-31 has not passed. (Timing note for later resolution: the election falls ~12.5 months after the statement, so the 'one more year' framing is approximately right on timing; the criterion turns solely on the government formed.)

statement: We have to find other ways to fund our transport system and the technology that's in use here, and what will very likely be a shift to electronic GPS-based road-user charges for all vehicles—a technology that's already in place for a significant section of our trucking fleet—will mean that petrol excise can be phased out and replaced with a much more comprehensive way of raising revenue based on people's real-time use of the transport network.
criterion: New Zealand legislation and NZTA implementation records. True if fuel excise duty has been phased out for light petrol vehicles and replaced by electronic road user charges applying to the general vehicle fleet; false if petrol excise remains the primary charging mechanism for light vehicles at the resolve-by date.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2030-12-31, far in the future. As of August 2026 fuel excise duty is still the primary charging mechanism for light petrol vehicles. Cabinet has agreed to legislative changes to move all ~3.5m light vehicles to electronic road user charges regardless of fuel type, with the Minister expecting the legislation to pass during 2026 and reporting pointing to a ~2027 start; light EVs lose their RUC exemption from 1 July 2026. No commencement date for universal light-vehicle RUC has been set, so neither the true nor false limb of the criterion is satisfied yet — the prediction is directionally on track but unresolved.

statement: That’s the key part to this: because we know that for planning purposes, having the congestion charge is great—it is going to change behaviours—but it’s really difficult for some people if there are not other options available to them.
criterion: Post-implementation evaluation of the Auckland congestion charging scheme by Auckland Transport / NZTA: true if the published evaluation reports a measurable reduction in peak-period vehicle trips in the charged area relative to the pre-scheme baseline; false if no measurable change in travel behaviour is found.
reasoning: The criterion requires a published post-implementation evaluation of an Auckland congestion charging scheme, but no such scheme is operating. The Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Bill passed Parliament on 11 November 2025 and comes into force in November 2026; Auckland Council is working toward a final scheme decision in early 2028, with ministerial approval and then several more years before operation. There is therefore no baseline, no charged area, and no evaluation to check. Resolve-by 2030-12-31 has not passed (and may still be early).

statement: It doesn’t mean to say that people are going to walk away from the Government, and, as I said, others will be opposed to this bill today.
criterion: The division record for the third reading of the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill, 21 October 2025. True if at least one party other than Labour voted against the bill; false if it passed with no party opposed.
reasoning: The Hansard third-reading record for 21 Oct 2025 ends 'Motion agreed to. Bill read a third time.' — no party vote/division was called, so the division record the criterion names does not exist. The debate record itself is decisive, however: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer stated Te Pati Maori's position as 'we definitely do not agree, and we do not support this bill', while Labour (with reservations), the Greens (Marama Davidson: 'The Green Party supports the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill'), National and NZ First supported it. So the criterion's false-condition — passed with no party opposed — is not met: a party other than Labour was opposed, exactly as Jackson predicted. Caveat: because the vote was taken on the voices, the opposition is documented by declared party positions in Hansard rather than by a recorded No vote.

statement: That means that there will be an estimated $90 million in economic benefit over the next decade from being able to have these conferences here.
criterion: Ministry for Regulation / MBIE regulatory impact and post-implementation material on the medical conferences amendment, plus conference-sector activity data for New Zealand 2026-2035. True if the cumulative economic benefit attributed to hosting these conferences over the decade is of the order of $90 million or more; false if the realised benefit is materially below that (e.g. under half), or if the conferences do not eventuate.
reasoning: The claim spans a decade and the criterion's resolve-by date is 2035-12-31; no cumulative benefit figure for 2026-2035 can exist yet (today is Aug 2026). Two contextual findings worth recording: (a) the Ministry for Regulation's own framing is that New Zealand 'could be missing out on as much as $90 million in potential revenue over the next few years', i.e. potential foregone revenue over a few years, not realised benefit over a decade as Seymour restated it; (b) the two conferences actually secured — ANZCA (May 2026, ~1,500 delegates, >$3m) and RANZCO (Nov 2026, ~1,800 delegates, >$2m) at the NZICC — amount to roughly $5m of economic activity, which is early data only and not sufficient to grade a ten-year cumulative figure either way.

statement: Therefore, the outcome from that is that patients still won't benefit from those medications.
criterion: Medsafe records of medicines approved under the two-jurisdiction pathway cross-referenced with Pharmac funding decisions and dispensing data; false if a material number of medicines approved via the new pathway are funded and dispensed to New Zealand patients, true if approvals under the pathway do not translate into funded, dispensed medicines.
reasoning: The criterion resolves by 2027-12-31 and requires Medsafe approvals under the two-jurisdiction ('rule of two') verification pathway cross-referenced with Pharmac funding and dispensing data. The Medicines Amendment Act 2025 commenced 19 Nov 2025, but the pathway only became operable when the Medicines (Consent by Verification) Rules 2026 came into force on 3 July 2026, roughly six weeks before this check. Consultation on those rules ran 16 Feb – 10 Apr 2026. I found no published list of medicines approved via the pathway, and therefore no funding or dispensing data to test against. Too early to grade; absence of approvals at six weeks is not evidence McLellan was right.

statement: In fact, what we believe 2026 will be is the tightening of and the changing of the guard—thank goodness—and the reclaiming of a pen to reshape the laws that this country needs to have.
criterion: The official 2026 New Zealand general election result and the government formed after it. True if the National-led coalition is replaced and a government including Labour/Greens/Te Pāti Māori takes office; false if the incumbent coalition is returned to government.
reasoning: The 2026 NZ general election is scheduled for 7 November 2026 and has not yet been held (today is 15 August 2026). The National/ACT/NZ First coalition under Christopher Luxon remains in office and campaigning is underway; no result or government formation exists to judge against the criterion, and the criterion's resolve-by date (2026-12-31) has not passed.

statement: I’m standing proudly in solidarity with our workers, including 100,000-plus workers who will be striking tomorrow across the country to send a clear message that they are not being valued by this Government and directly impacted by the decisions of this Government.
criterion: Union (NZNO, PSA, NZEI/PPTA) and media participation figures for the strike action on 23 October 2025; true if reported participation is at or above 100,000 workers, false if materially below.
reasoning: The 23 October 2025 'mega strike' proceeded as planned and reported participation met or exceeded 100,000. RNZ reported 'More than 100,000 workers go on strike'; Labor Notes reported as many as 110,000 (~60,000 teachers, 30,000+ nurses, 5,000 doctors, ~20,000 other health workers), the largest NZ industrial action since 1979. Pre-strike union ballots corroborate the total (NZNO ~36,000 Te Whatu Ora nurses/HCAs/midwives, NZEI ~40,000 primary teachers/principals/support staff, PSA ~11,500 mental health and allied health workers, plus PPTA and ASMS). Checked for disconfirming evidence: no union withdrew and no source disputes the figure. 1News's 'tens of thousands' headline refers to rally attendance (Wellington and South Island events were curtailed by red weather warnings), not strike participation.

statement: I think in the future we're going to put more different assets into the fund as well.
criterion: Auckland Future Fund annual reports and Auckland Council Long-Term Plan documents; true if any fund or asset beyond the original Auckland Airport share sale proceeds has been transferred into the AFF by the resolve-by date, false if the fund still holds only the airport proceeds and their reinvested returns.
reasoning: The criterion resolves by 2028-06-30, nearly two years away. As of now the Auckland Future Fund's only capital contribution remains the $1.32b Auckland International Airport shareholding, settled 4 December 2024 (per the annual report for the 9 months ended 30 June 2025; the FY2026 report is not yet published, due by 30 September 2026). The port lease originally intended as the second tranche was abandoned in November 2024 when Mayor Wayne Brown adopted a $1.1b/10-year profit-contribution plan keeping Port of Auckland under council ownership — that is a dividend stream to the council, not a transfer into the fund. An Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill had its second reading on 8 October 2025 and could enable future contributions. Absence of a further transfer today does not make the prediction wrong before its resolve-by date.

statement: State Highway 6 is a vital connection for people and goods, will boost economic growth in Nelson-Tasman, reduce peak journey times through Richmond by at least 10 minutes by 2034, and of course developments continue on the Belfast to Pegasus and Woodend Bypass road of national significance, with a fast-track application being worked through currently.
criterion: NZTA journey-time monitoring data for the State Highway 6 corridor through Richmond; true if the average peak journey time in 2034 is at least 10 minutes lower than the 2025 baseline, false if the reduction is under 10 minutes or peak times are unchanged/worse.
reasoning: The claim restates NZTA's published benefit for the SH6 Hope Bypass / Richmond corridor: 'reduce peak travel times through Richmond by at least 10 minutes by 2034' (and 16 minutes by 2054), and the Belfast to Pegasus / Woodend Bypass RoNS was indeed proceeding with a fast-track application in late 2025. The criterion requires NZTA journey-time monitoring for the corridor in 2034 against a 2025 baseline; that data cannot exist yet, and the resolve-by date is 2034-12-31. Contextual risk worth noting but not resolving: in October 2025 the investment case split the bypass into two stages with tolling recommended, and the cost estimate has grown to $1.1-1.4b, so delivery by 2034 is not assured.

statement: Those wait-lists are only going to increase with tomorrow's strikes.
criterion: Health New Zealand planned care / elective wait-list reporting and its published count of appointments and procedures deferred because of the 23 October 2025 strike. True if Health NZ reports deferred appointments or procedures attributable to the strike and the wait-list count rises across the period covering it; false if no material deferrals are recorded or the wait-list count does not rise.
reasoning: First leg of the criterion holds: Health NZ told RNZ before the 23 October 2025 mega strike that it would cancel more than 900 procedures and wipe more than 1,380 first specialist assessments from the schedule, and deferred appointments were rebooked afterwards. The second leg fails. The elective treatment waiting list did not rise across the period covering the strike: ASMS's May 2026 report (a union source, not government spin) records 6,470 (7.6%) FEWER people on the elective treatment waiting list in December 2025 than December 2024; Health NZ's October-December 2025 quarter (the quarter containing the strike) reported 51,513 people treated from the elective waitlist, up from 46,841 a year earlier, 64.5% treated within four months (up from 59.2%), 179,816 FSAs completed (up from 167,917) and 62.2% seen within four months (up from 60.6%); and the list has fallen from a peak of over 80,000 to around 75,000. I checked for the disconfirming case (a level rise Oct->Dec 2025 masked by a year-on-year fall) and found no reporting of one; every published series points down. The criterion states the claim is false if the wait-list count does not rise, so a one-day four-hour strike producing ~2,300 deferrals inside a quarter of improving throughput does not meet it.

statement: There’s going to be growing migration, growing business liquidations.
criterion: Stats NZ migration estimates and NZ Companies Office / Centrix liquidation counts for the 12 months from October 2025; true if both outward migration and liquidations rise relative to the preceding 12 months, false if either falls.
reasoning: The liquidations leg is correct and then some: Centrix recorded about 3,023 companies into liquidation in the year to March 2026, an 11-year high, up roughly 14% on the prior year, with 286 in March 2026 alone (worst March in 11 years); construction 768, hospitality 399 (+49%), retail +34%, transport +27%. Business failures kept rising through mid-2026. The migration leg fails on the criterion as written, which requires outward migration to rise. Stats NZ reports migrant departures of 113,100 in the June 2026 year, a 5 percent FALL from 118,800 in the June 2025 year, with the net migration gain rising to 17,600 from 10,300 precisely because fewer people left; NZ-citizen departures also eased (62,800 in the March 2026 year, net loss ~36,500, below the 2025 peaks). Nine of the criterion's twelve months are covered and the 5,700-departure gap would need an implausible surge in Jul-Oct 2026 to reverse, so I have not treated this as not_yet_due; final Stats NZ data for the full Oct 2025-Oct 2026 window lands around December 2026. Note one ambiguity: read as 'net migration will grow', the claim would be true, but in context Edmonds was listing signs of economic deterioration, i.e. people leaving, and the criterion binds to outward migration.

statement: The life expectancy for people will get longer and longer and they will need to continue to think about the ways that they can contribute to society.
criterion: Stats NZ New Zealand period life tables (life expectancy at birth): true if the figure published in a release after this statement exceeds the most recent figure available at the time of speaking, false if it is flat or lower.
reasoning: At the time of speaking (22 Oct 2025) the most recent Stats NZ period life table was National and subnational period life tables: 2022-2024, released 30 July 2025, giving life expectancy at birth of 80.1 years (males) and 83.5 (females). A period life table published after the statement — the abridged period life table in Births and deaths: year ended December 2025, released 17 February 2026 — gives 2023-2025 life expectancy at birth of 80.4 (males) and 83.7 (females), which Stats NZ explicitly notes is 0.3 years higher than 2022-2024. The criterion's test (a post-statement release exceeding the figure available at the time of speaking) is met for both sexes. Note the criterion is a short-horizon proxy for a long-run 'longer and longer' claim; judged as written, it passes.

statement: I really am concerned that if this bill goes through with the title Life Jackets for Children and Young Persons Bill, we will be advised that changing the age will not be within the scope of the bill.
criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report on the Life Jackets for Children and Young Persons Bill, plus the departmental/Clerk's scope advice published with it; true if the committee is advised that raising or removing the age limit is outside the bill's scope, false if the committee is advised the age threshold may be amended within scope (or amends it).
reasoning: The scope constraint Wade-Brown named was real: raising/removing the under-15 age limit was treated as an out-of-scope amendment, so the Transport and Infrastructure Committee had to seek Business Committee permission under Standing Orders before it could proceed. But the consequence she feared did not follow. Permission was granted, the committee broadened the bill to all ages in March 2026, reopened public submissions (closing 15 April 2026), and reported back on 13 July 2026 with unanimous cross-party support — the bill returning to the House renamed the Maritime Transport (Lifejackets on Recreational Craft) Amendment Bill. The criterion's false branch ('or amends it') is therefore satisfied, while its true branch (advised the change is outside scope) also holds, so the prediction is half right: correct that the age change was outside scope as introduced, wrong that this would prevent the age from being changed.

statement: I relish the opportunity to reply and thank the members for their contributions and the overwhelming majority of parliamentarians that will be supporting this to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee.
criterion: The division record for the first reading of the Life Jackets for Children and Young Persons Bill; true if the bill passed and was referred to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee with well over a simple majority (ACT's votes the main opposition), false if it failed or the vote was close.
reasoning: The first reading division on 22 October 2025 recorded Ayes 106 (National 49, Labour 34, Greens 15, NZ First 8) and Noes 11 (ACT New Zealand). The motion was agreed to and the bill was referred to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee, which subsequently considered it and reported back in July 2026. This is well over a simple majority (106 of 117 votes cast), with ACT as the sole opposing party — matching the criterion in every particular, including its expectation that ACT would be the main opposition.

statement: I just want to note that this bill’s probably unanimous passing should be a more frequent occurrence in this House.
criterion: The voting record for the third reading of the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill in the New Zealand House of Representatives. True if the bill passed with no party or member voting against; false if any party or member is recorded as opposed.
reasoning: The bill passed, but not unanimously. On the same sitting day as the quote (8 Oct 2025), the second-reading party vote was Ayes 116 (National 49, Labour 34, Green 14, ACT 11, NZ First 8) to Noes 5 (Te Pati Maori), with Mariameno Kapa-Kingi stating Te Pati Maori 'can no longer continue that support' because of the lack of Maori representation in the fund's governance. The bill was read a third time on 12 Nov 2025 and received Royal assent on 18 Nov 2025 as the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Act 2025. Limitation: the third-reading division record the criterion names could not be retrieved (parliament.nz Hansard returns a bot-protection page, Scoop has not mirrored that debate, and WhereTheyStand records no breakdown for the 3rd reading). The verdict therefore rests on the recorded second-reading party vote and Te Pati Maori's explicit, structural withdrawal of support, with no evidence of a reversal. Marked wrong rather than partly_correct because the criterion is explicitly binary on any party being recorded opposed — though in fairness the margin was 116-5 and the speaker hedged with 'probably'.

statement: I would take a little bit of issue with Cameron Luxton's take on lifting the super age; I don't think that's going anywhere fast, but we're here.
criterion: Parliamentary bills register and Government policy announcements: false if a bill or Government policy raising the New Zealand Superannuation eligibility age above 65 is introduced to the House or adopted as Government policy before 31 December 2027; true if no such bill or policy is introduced or adopted by that date.
reasoning: The criterion's window runs to 31 December 2027 and today is 16 August 2026, so it cannot resolve yet. Status so far is consistent with the prediction: the NZ Superannuation eligibility age remains 65, no bill raising it above 65 has been introduced to the House, and no Government policy raising it has been adopted — NZ First's opposition inside the coalition is the stated block, even though Finance Minister Nicola Willis and ACT favour a rise. However, National is campaigning on lifting the age (Luxon confirming a policy similar to the 2017 'to 67 by 2040' plan) at the general election set for 7 November 2026, so a bill or adopted Government policy before 31 Dec 2027 remains live and would flip this to wrong.

statement: Look, congratulations to the member Carl Bates on getting your bill drawn, and it looks like it will have unanimous support from the House.
criterion: The division/voice-vote record for the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill's subsequent readings in the NZ House; true if it passes with no party recorded against, false if any party votes against.
reasoning: The bill passed — second reading 22 Oct 2025, third reading 18 Feb 2026, Royal assent 19 Feb 2026, in force 21 Feb 2026 as the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Act 2026 — but not with unanimous support. At the very second reading Hernandez was speaking in, Te Pati Maori opposed it: Oriini Kaipara spoke for the party against the bill, arguing not everyone has equal health and that many Maori in that age bracket are 'very frail'. Context: the first reading on 9 April 2025 was Ayes 102 (National 49, Labour 34, ACT 11, NZ First 8) to Noes 21 (Green 15, Te Pati Maori 6); the Greens switched to support after select committee, which is likely what prompted the 'unanimous' read, but Te Pati Maori did not. Limitation: exact second- and third-reading division totals were not retrievable (parliament.nz Hansard is behind bot protection; WhereTheyStand records no breakdown for either reading), so the Te Pati Maori opposition rests on Newsroom's 26 Nov 2025 report of the second reading, accessed via search-indexed content after a direct fetch returned 403.

statement: Unfortunately, it’s going to have a short life.
criterion: The Hansard division record for the first reading of the member's bill debated on 22 October 2025; true if the bill was defeated at first reading, false if it passed and was referred to select committee.
reasoning: The bill debated on 22 October 2025 was Julie Anne Genter's Crown Minerals (Prohibition on Coal Mining) Amendment Bill (145-1). The Hansard record of the first reading division shows Ayes 55 (Labour 34, Green 15, Te Pati Maori 6), Noes 68 (National 49, ACT 11, NZ First 8), with the Deputy Speaker declaring 'Motion not agreed to.' The bill was defeated at first reading and was never referred to select committee, which is exactly the criterion's condition for true. The NZ Minerals Council independently described the bill as 'rejected at first reading' on 23 October 2025.
