No single attack or massacre with a higher toll is on record.

statement: We are encouraged that the United States-led peace plan—supported by Muslim countries around the world, including Saudi Arabia, Jordan, UAE, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, Qatar, and Egypt—represents a possible first step to achieving these goals.
criterion: Public statements by the governments of Saudi Arabia, Jordan, the UAE, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, Qatar and Egypt regarding the US-led Gaza peace plan, dated on or before 7 October 2025 (e.g. any joint communiqué or foreign-ministry release). True if all eight are on record supporting or welcoming it; false if any named country did not.
reasoning: On 29 September 2025 — eight days before the quote — the foreign ministers of Qatar, Jordan, the UAE, Indonesia, Pakistan, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Egypt issued a joint statement welcoming President Trump's leadership and his proposal to end the war in Gaza, rebuild it, prevent displacement and advance a comprehensive peace. That is precisely the eight countries Peters named, all eight on the record supporting/welcoming the plan before 7 October 2025. Published on the Qatari, Emirati and Pakistani foreign ministry sites.

statement: Well, we can report that we have not received criticism from partners or from other countries near to, or far from, the Middle East.
criterion: Public statements, démarches or diplomatic communications from any foreign government criticising New Zealand's decision not to recognise Palestinian statehood, between the national statement in New York (late September 2025) and 7 October 2025. False if any such statement from a partner or other government is on the record; true if none is found.
reasoning: Searched for foreign-government criticism of NZ's 27 September 2025 non-recognition decision between the UN statement and 7 October 2025, from several angles: Palestinian representatives (incl. the General Delegation of Palestine to Australia/NZ), Turkey, Malaysia, Indonesia, and the recognising partners Australia, UK and Canada. Every critic on the record in that window is domestic or civil-society — Helen Clark, Labour, the Greens, Dayenu, NZ Palestinians — including in Anadolu's 'Day of Shame' piece, which names only NZ political figures. No foreign-government statement, demarche or communique criticising NZ was found; conversely, Israel's ambassador to NZ publicly praised the decision, and NZ Herald reported Peters saying he had yet to hear from other countries apart from Pacific leaders who congratulated him. Caveat: this is a negative claim about largely private diplomatic channels, so the finding is 'none on the public record', not proof none was received.

statement: Now, three New Zealanders are being held by the Israeli Government and are awaiting deportation.
criterion: MFAT consular statements and contemporaneous reporting on New Zealand citizens detained by Israel after the October 2025 flotilla interception. True if the number held and awaiting deportation on 7 October 2025 was three; false if it was a different number.
reasoning: Three New Zealand citizens — Rana Hamida, Youssef Sammour and Samuel Leason — were detained after Israeli forces intercepted the Global Sumud Flotilla on 1–2 October 2025. Contemporaneous RNZ reporting (6–7 Oct) states they were to be deported from Israel to Jordan on Wednesday 8 October; Jordanian state news confirmed their arrival in Jordan on 8 October, and they landed at Auckland on Friday 10 October. So on 7 October 2025 the number held by Israel and awaiting deportation was three, exactly as stated. No source names a fourth NZ detainee from this interception (the 'up to six New Zealanders' figure belongs to a separate April 2026 interception). Minor caveat: Peters was himself the on-record source for the deportation timing, but the count of three and the timeline are independently corroborated by family/activist accounts and Jordanian reporting.

statement: Now, what’s fascinating about that question is that there was a poll where 60 percent of New Zealanders did not express support for recognition. It was almost as though that majority is of no moment; 60 percent did not express it. And it was followed up by a Stuff poll that said 55:45 percent against recognition until it was distorted by people voting countless times. So to make the statement that New Zealanders in the majority are for recognition is demonstrably numerically wrong.
criterion: Published New Zealand polling on recognition of Palestinian statehood in 2025 (e.g. Curia, Talbot Mills, Research NZ, or the Stuff self-select poll referenced), with the reported question wording and response breakdown. True if a poll reports 60 percent not expressing support and a Stuff poll reports 55:45 against; false if the published figures or the question wording materially differ.
reasoning: The poll Peters refers to is RNZ-Reid Research (n=1000, online, 4–12 Sept 2025, MoE ±3.1%), question 'Should New Zealand recognise a Palestinian state?': 42.5% yes, 22.1% no, 35.4% don't know. The published figure for 'did not express support' is therefore 57.5%, not 60% — and 35.4 points of that are undecided, not opposed; actual opposition is 22.1%. The NZ Herald noted at the time that Peters 'took that as meaning that 60 per cent (57.5%) did not support recognition', i.e. the 60% is his own rounding of a re-cut that folds don't-knows into opposition. On the second limb, I could find no published Stuff poll reporting 55:45 against recognition, nor any published note about repeat voting distorting it. Stuff's own reported polling in September 2025 ran the other way ('Poll shows what voters think about NZ recognising... plurality voters think NZ should recognise Palestinian statehood'); the only Stuff self-select item is a reader callout ('We asked for your thoughts on NZ's stance on a Palestinian state', 29 Sept) with no published breakdown. His narrow conclusion does hold: no published poll shows an outright majority (>50%) for recognition — 42.5% is a plurality. Substance partly holds, figures materially differ from what was published, and the Stuff figure is unverifiable.

statement: Israel’s treatment of humanitarian flotillas has been heavy-handed and unlawful.
criterion: Determinations by competent legal bodies on the October 2025 flotilla interceptions — UN Human Rights Council / OHCHR findings, UN special rapporteur assessments, or ICJ/court rulings — together with the recorded position of the vessels when boarded relative to territorial waters under UNCLOS. True if authoritative legal assessment finds the interceptions unlawful (e.g. boarding in international waters without lawful basis); false if they are found lawful under the naval-blockade rules.
reasoning: Position when boarded: the Global Sumud Flotilla vessels were intercepted 1–2 October 2025 roughly 70–120 nautical miles from Gaza, and the 8 October Conscience interception likewise occurred on the high seas — in every case far outside the 12 nm territorial sea and 24 nm contiguous zone under UNCLOS. Legal assessment: the criterion names UN special rapporteur assessments as qualifying, and they found the interceptions unlawful — Irene Khan (OHCHR press release, 8 Oct 2025) called it 'an attack against unarmed civilians on the high seas… yet another violation of international law by Israel', and Francesca Albanese called the operations 'yet another act of piracy by the Israeli army in international waters'. Scholarly analysis (EJIL:Talk) concludes the enforcement distance has no post-1945 precedent and so cannot be lawful blockade enforcement. 'Heavy-handed' is supported by detainee accounts of abuse (disputed by Israel's foreign ministry) and by the Palmer Report's earlier finding of excessive force at Mavi Marmara. Disconfirming evidence checked: the counter-case is real and substantial — the 2011 UN Secretary-General's Palmer Panel found Israel's naval blockade lawful in principle with a right to visit, search and capture in international waters, and experts including Robbie Sabel and Yuval Shany defend interception under San Remo blockade rules. But no court or competent body has found the October 2025 interceptions lawful, so the criterion's false-condition is not met while its true-condition is. Scored true on the criterion as written, with the caveat that the legality question is contested and unadjudicated rather than settled.

statement: Further to the Minister, does the Minister agree that New Zealand was put on notice in 2024 by the International Court of Justice that it had a legal obligation to prevent genocide in Gaza, that is not necessary for a definitive determination on genocide to be made before action is taken, and what actions has the Government taken to prevent genocide in Gaza?
criterion: The text of the ICJ's provisional measures orders in South Africa v Israel (26 January 2024 and 28 March 2024), plus the Court's statement of third-State obligations under the Genocide Convention; true if the Court in 2024 found a plausible risk of genocide and stated that States parties' duty to prevent is engaged without a definitive merits determination, false if no such finding or statement exists.
reasoning: Two of three elements hold, one does not. HOLDS: the ICJ's 26 January 2024 provisional measures order (para. 54) found plausible at least some rights claimed by South Africa, including the right of Palestinians in Gaza to be protected from acts of genocide, and ordered Israel to prevent genocidal acts; the 28 March and 24 May 2024 orders reinforced this. HOLDS: no definitive determination of genocide is required before a duty to act arises — but this is the holding of Bosnia v Serbia (2007) para. 431 ('the obligation to prevent, and the corresponding duty to act, arise at the instant that the State learns of... a serious risk that genocide will be committed'), not something the Court said in 2024; the 2024 orders expressly do not prejudge the merits and no merits judgment exists (the case is still in written pleadings, time-limits extended through 2025-26). FAILS: the ICJ did not in 2024 put New Zealand or any third State on notice of a legal obligation to prevent genocide in Gaza. The provisional measures are addressed to Israel. The only passage concerning other States parties is para. 33's erga omnes partes language, which establishes standing to invoke another State party's responsibility, not a duty to prevent. Commentary (SOAS, EJIL:Talk!, University of Auckland) presents the third-State duty as an inference from the Convention's erga omnes character plus prior jurisprudence, explicitly not as a holding of the January 2024 order. The criterion required both a plausible-risk finding AND a Court statement that States parties' duty to prevent is engaged absent a merits determination; only the first is satisfied, so the substance is real but materially overstated by attributing the third-State notice to the ICJ.

statement: Helen Clark had nine years to recognise Palestine; she didn’t. Jacinda Ardern had five years to recognise Palestine; she didn’t. Mr Hipkins had a year to recognise Palestine and he didn’t.
criterion: Prime ministerial tenure dates (Clark 1999–2008, Ardern 2017–2023, Hipkins 2023) and the MFAT/New Zealand Government record of formal recognition of the State of Palestine; true if none of the three governments extended recognition and the stated durations are approximately right, false if any did or the durations are materially wrong.
reasoning: New Zealand has never extended formal recognition to the State of Palestine, and did not do so under any of the three leaders named. MFAT maintains a long-standing policy of not making formal acts of recognition or non-recognition of states; as of Winston Peters' 27 September 2025 UNGA announcement NZ still had not recognised Palestine, confirming no prior government had. The two nearest historical acts fall short of recognition and were not under these leaders' relevant framing: 1988 recognition of the Palestine Information Office as PLO representative, and the November 2012 UN vote for Palestine's non-member observer state status (under the Key government). Durations are approximately right: Clark 10 Dec 1999 - 19 Nov 2008 (~8 years 11 months, fairly stated as nine); Ardern 26 Oct 2017 - 25 Jan 2023 (~5 years 3 months, five); Hipkins 25 Jan - 27 Nov 2023 (~10 months, loosely 'a year' - the only mild rounding-up, not material). Disconfirming check: no record of any NZ government act of recognition, and Labour only called for recognition in April 2024, from opposition.

statement: The reality is, there has been no International Court of Justice ruling to that effect. Or does he think that we should just ignore the International Court of Justice and just come to our own interpretation, legally qualified or otherwise?
criterion: The ICJ docket in South Africa v Israel and any advisory opinions to 7 October 2025; true if no ICJ ruling has determined that New Zealand holds a legal obligation to prevent genocide in Gaza, false if such a ruling or order exists.
reasoning: Checked the full ICJ docket in South Africa v Israel (case 192) and the advisory opinions to 7 October 2025. No ruling determines that New Zealand holds a legal obligation to prevent genocide in Gaza. The provisional measures orders of 26 January, 28 March and 24 May 2024 are addressed to Israel; no merits judgment has been delivered (only time-limit orders in April 2025, October 2025 and May 2026). The erga omnes partes passage at para. 33 of the January 2024 order concerns standing to invoke another State party's responsibility, not a third State's duty to prevent. Disconfirming check: the 19 July 2024 advisory opinion on the Occupied Palestinian Territory does impose obligations on all States, but these are non-recognition of the unlawful situation, non-assistance and cooperation to end it, arising from the illegality of the occupation - not a genocide-prevention duty. Caveat worth recording though outside the criterion: NZ's duty to prevent under Article I of the Genocide Convention is a treaty obligation independent of any ICJ ruling, and Bosnia v Serbia (2007) para. 431 holds it arises on awareness of serious risk, so the absence of a Gaza-specific ruling does not entail the absence of an obligation. As worded against the criterion, the claim is accurate.

statement: Let us be clear that recognising Palestinian Statehood, the likes of which the Green Party put forward a motion to propose to do exactly that in 2021, was opposed by National and ACT MPs, is an important part of being very clear that Israel must not be rewarded for its genocide.
criterion: The 2021 Hansard record for a Green Party motion or request for leave on recognising Palestinian statehood; true if such a motion was put and National and/or ACT members objected or voted against, false if no such motion exists or if the objection came from elsewhere.
reasoning: The motion exists: Golriz Ghahraman sought leave on 19 May 2021 for Parliament to 'recognise and support the right of Palestine to self-determination and statehood, and recognise the State of Palestine among our community of nations'. It required unanimous leave and was blocked. National and ACT both refused to support it (ACT: 'not a helpful contribution to this discourse'; National: supported a two-state solution but 'didn't feel this motion would be helpful'), which satisfies the criterion's 'National and/or ACT objected' test. However, Labour — then the governing party — also declined, with Nanaia Mahuta citing the motion's wording. Davidson's attribution of the blocking to National and ACT MPs alone omits the decisive objector, so the substance holds but is materially incomplete. Also a leave request refused by objection, not a recorded vote.

statement: Because any world that normalises over 20,000 - plus children’s lives being taken by the violence of Israel, any State—any country—that normalises the intentional killing of doctors and nurses and journalists and the winding back of the health system, surely, that needs to be part of our responsibility.
criterion: Gaza Ministry of Health and UN OCHA casualty data as at October 2025 for deaths of children; true if the recorded figure exceeds 20,000, false if it is materially below that.
reasoning: The criterion's named sources carry the figure. OCHA's Humanitarian Situation Update #329 (published 9 October 2025) cites the Gaza Ministry of Health breakdown published on 7 October 2025 — the same day as the speech: of 67,173 Palestinians killed between 7 October 2023 and 7 October 2025, 20,179 were children (30 per cent), of whom 1,029 were under one year old and 5,031 under five. The 20,000 threshold had already been reported by Save the Children on 6 September 2025 (Gaza Government Media Office data), and Wikipedia's compilation records 19,424 children as at 3 September 2025 — a trajectory consistent with 20,179 by 7 October. The recorded figure therefore exceeds 20,000 as at the date of the statement. (Only the numerical claim is assessed here; the characterisations of intent and 'genocide' are outside the criterion.)

statement: It has democracies in 19 years of consistent free fall, where now autocratic regimes are more plentiful than democracies that we support; more plentiful than countries that foster and use the democratic process.
criterion: The Freedom House Freedom in the World 2025 report; true if it records a 19th consecutive year of decline in global freedom and shows authoritarian states outnumbering democracies on its own classification, false if the run of decline is a different length or the balance of regime types is the other way.
reasoning: The first half is exactly right: Freedom House's Freedom in the World 2025 records the 19th consecutive year of decline in global freedom, with 60 countries deteriorating and 34 improving in 2024. The second half fails against the same report. On Freedom House's own classification, democracies still outnumber authoritarian states by count: it rated 106 of 195 countries as electoral democracies in 2024 (down from 110), a majority, and 'Free' countries outnumber 'Not Free' ones. The claim that autocracies are now more numerous than democracies comes from V-Dem, not Freedom House. Cameron's statement is true if measured by population (Freedom House reports 40 per cent of the world lives in Not Free countries versus 20 per cent in Free ones), but he said 'more plentiful', which is a count of countries — a reading he did not signal.

statement: But this didn’t start on 7 October 2023, and I think that we have to remind ourselves of what happened 75 years ago, when Palestinian land was taken, when houses were destroyed, and when people were displaced and, in fact, their self-determination—their mana motuhake—was denied.
criterion: The historical record of the 1948 Palestine war/Nakba (UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine and UNRWA displacement figures, standard scholarly surveys). True if land was expropriated, villages destroyed and a large Palestinian population displaced in that period; false if the record does not show this. Note the stated interval: 75 years before October 2025 is 1950, while the events referred to are 1948.
reasoning: The historical record supports every substantive element. UNRWA/UN records: more than 700,000 Palestinians displaced from their towns and villages in 1948; standard surveys (Khalidi; Al Jazeera's mapping) count 400-600 Palestinian villages destroyed, ~530 between 1947-49; land was expropriated and the population's self-determination denied. UNRWA and the UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine were both established by the General Assembly in 1949 precisely to address this displacement. The criterion's flagged interval issue is real but immaterial: 75 years before Oct 2025 is 1950, while the events are 1948 (77 years) - a round-number slip in a rhetorical aside, not an overstatement of substance (the UN itself used '75 years' for the same events in May 2023). The criterion's true/false test is whether the record shows expropriation, destruction and large-scale displacement in that period; it does.

statement: We acknowledge the three New Zealanders who were detained by Israel after being illegally intercepted in international waters, because they had the courage to actually do what this Government doesn’t.
criterion: Contemporaneous reporting and MFAT/NZ government statements on the Global Sumud Flotilla interception of early October 2025. True if exactly three New Zealand citizens were detained by Israeli authorities after the interception; false if the number differs or none were detained. The 'illegally … in international waters' element resolves against the recorded interception coordinates and the legal characterisation given by the UN human rights bodies or relevant courts.
reasoning: Exactly three New Zealand citizens - Rana Hamida, Youssef Sammour and Samuel Leason - were detained after Israeli forces intercepted the Global Sumud Flotilla on 1-2 October 2025. Foreign Minister Winston Peters himself confirmed the number when announcing their deportation from Israel to Jordan on Wednesday 8 October; they arrived back in Auckland on Friday 10 October. On the qualifiers: the first vessels were boarded about 70 nautical miles from Gaza (the last, Marinette, at ~42.5nm on 3 Oct), far outside the 12nm territorial sea, so 'international waters' is established on the recorded positions. On 'illegally', the criterion permits resolution against UN human rights bodies: Special Rapporteur Irene Khan called it 'yet another violation of international law by Israel' and Francesca Albanese called it 'an act of piracy... in international waters'; no court has ruled on it. Caution: searches surface RNZ reports of 'up to six New Zealanders' detained (O'Connor, Taher, Blondel, Janssen) - those concern the 2026 flotilla, months after this speech, and do not bear on the October 2025 count.

statement: There was a statement made there about genocide that is not authorised, supported, or precedented by any international court whatsoever, but they make the statement anyway, and, sadly, that’s been far too often the case on this very, very sad issue.
criterion: The orders and rulings of the ICJ and ICC concerning Gaza up to October 2025. True if no international court has issued any finding or order lending support to a genocide characterisation; false if such an order exists — e.g. the ICJ's provisional measures orders in South Africa v Israel (January, March and May 2024) finding a plausible risk to rights under the Genocide Convention.
reasoning: The criterion's named falsifier exists. The ICJ issued three provisional measures orders in South Africa v. Israel (Application of the Genocide Convention in the Gaza Strip): 26 January 2024, 28 March 2024 and 24 May 2024. In the January order the Court held that 'at least some of the rights claimed by South Africa are plausible' - those rights being the right of Palestinians in Gaza not to be subjected to acts of genocide - and ordered Israel to take all measures within its power to prevent genocidal acts and to prevent and punish incitement to genocide. The 24 May 2024 order, by 13 votes to 2, directed Israel to halt any action in Rafah 'which may inflict on the Palestinian group in Gaza conditions of life that could bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part'. Peters is correct on the narrowest point - no international court had made a merits finding of genocide by October 2025, the case being still at the pleadings stage - but that is not what he claimed. 'Supported, or precedented by any international court whatsoever' is directly contradicted by binding orders premised on plausible Genocide Convention rights.

statement: Well, here’s the reality: there are clear guidelines out in the 1990s Montevideo Convention on recognition, which is not met.
criterion: The Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States — its date of signature (public treaty record) and its four stated criteria for statehood, applied to Palestine. True if the Convention dates from the 1990s and Palestine plainly fails those criteria; false if the Convention dates from another decade, or if the application of the criteria is genuinely contested among states that have recognised Palestine.
reasoning: The Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States was signed at Montevideo on 26 December 1933 and entered into force in 1934 — not the 1990s, six decades off. The criterion's second false condition is also met: the application of the four criteria (permanent population, defined territory, government, capacity to enter into relations with other states) to Palestine is genuinely contested, not plainly failed. By late September 2025 at least 151 of 193 UN members recognised the State of Palestine (157 by October 2025, including four of five permanent Security Council members), and the academic literature finds Palestine largely satisfies the criteria with only the 'effective government' limb seriously disputed. Note also that the Convention codifies the declarative theory, under which statehood is expressly 'independent of recognition by the other states' — so citing it as a guideline governing recognition inverts what it says.

statement: You’ve got these Muslim countries: Saudi Arabia, Jordan, United Arab Emirates, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, Qatar, and Egypt all seeking to work with the American-led peace plan to get a solution.
criterion: Public statements by the governments named — Saudi Arabia, Jordan, the UAE, Indonesia, Pakistan, Türkiye, Qatar and Egypt — from September–October 2025 on the US-led Gaza plan, including any joint statement. True if all eight publicly endorsed or engaged with the plan; false if any of the eight had not.
reasoning: On 29 September 2025 — eight days before the statement — the foreign ministers of exactly the eight named states issued a joint statement welcoming President Trump's leadership and 'his sincere efforts to end the war in Gaza', welcoming his announced proposal to end the war, rebuild Gaza and prevent displacement, and reaffirming 'their joint commitment to work with the United States' on a comprehensive deal. The signatory list published by both the Qatari and Emirati foreign ministries is Qatar, Jordan, UAE, Indonesia, Pakistan, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Egypt — an exact match for Peters' list, with no member of the eight absent or dissenting. Checked for the opposite: no evidence any of the eight declined or withheld engagement in the September–October 2025 window; the same eight later continued to act as a bloc on the plan's implementation.

statement: And might I say, on the so-called aid programme, the flotilla was offered—by the Italian Government—a military ship to take all of their so-called aid on those boats and to make sure they got to the destination. Guess what? They refused it.
criterion: Italian government statements and contemporaneous reporting on the Global Sumud Flotilla, late September 2025. True if Italy offered a navy vessel to carry the flotilla's aid to its destination and the flotilla declined; false if no such offer was made, if the offer was on materially different terms (e.g. transfer of aid to a third party rather than delivery to Gaza), or if it was accepted.
reasoning: The statement conflates two distinct Italian actions. (1) Italy did send a navy frigate (the Fasan, later a second vessel) on 24 September 2025, but Defence Minister Crosetto deployed it for 'possible relief, assistance and protection' after the drone attacks of 23–24 September — not to carry the flotilla's cargo. It escorted the boats and withdrew on 30 September as they neared Gaza. (2) The offer the flotilla actually refused was Meloni's and Crosetto's mediation proposal to unload the aid in Cyprus and hand it to the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem, which would pass it to Israel for delivery into Gaza. Organisers rejected it, telling CNN they 'will not be accepting the offer to give the aid to anyone other than the intended recipients, which are the civilians in Gaza'. That is precisely the disqualifying scenario the criterion names: transfer of aid to a third party rather than an Italian military ship delivering it to the destination. The refusal happened; the terms as described did not.

statement: When he launched a marketing campaign claiming that “Everyone must go”, was he suggesting that everyone who can’t find work in New Zealand must go to Australia to find work, as jobs disappear in New Zealand and 200 New Zealanders a day, under his leadership, give up and leave the country?
criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics, NZ-citizen departures for the most recent annual period before October 2025; true if the annual figure is at or above ~73,000 (200/day), false if materially lower.
reasoning: Criterion: NZ-citizen departures for the most recent annual period before Oct 2025, true if >= ~73,000 (200/day). As published at the time, Stats NZ's provisional estimate for the July 2025 year was 73,300 NZ-citizen migrant departures (200.8/day) — a record on the current series — so Hipkins accurately quoted the then-official statistic (the Aug 2025 year, 73,900, was not released until ~14 Oct 2025, after he spoke). However, these provisional estimates are built on the 12/16-month rule with machine-learning predictions for recent months and have since been revised down materially. Stats NZ data as at 13 Feb 2026 show calendar-year NZ-citizen departures of 65,792 (2023), 67,221 (2024) and 66,309 (2025), implying ~66,500 for the year to mid-2025, i.e. ~182/day — about 9-10% below the criterion's threshold. AAP's April 2026 fact check confirms the revised peak was 67,812 in the year to April 2024, below the Feb 2012 record of 72,401, and notes the initial 2023-2024 'record' estimates were revised down. Substance (a near-decade-high outflow of New Zealanders) holds; the specific 200-a-day figure is overstated against the settled data.

statement: Well, I mean, the member can play politics with it as much as he likes, but the reality is that the number of New Zealanders leaving New Zealand is the same as it was in the last year that he was Prime Minister.
criterion: Stats NZ international migration series, NZ-citizen departures for the year to Dec 2023 compared with the year to the most recent month before Oct 2025; true if the two are within a few percent, false if the later figure is materially higher or lower.
reasoning: Criterion: compare NZ-citizen departures for the year to Dec 2023 (Hipkins' last year as PM — he held office Jan-Nov 2023) with the year to the most recent month before Oct 2025; true if within a few percent. On Stats NZ's current estimates (Figure.NZ series sourced from Stats NZ, updated 13 Feb 2026), NZ-citizen migrant departures were 65,792 in the 2023 year, 67,221 in 2024 and 66,309 in 2025, so the annual figure for the year to mid-2025 sits around 66,500 — within roughly 1-2% of the 2023 figure. That is 'the same' by any reasonable reading. Important caveat on timing: when Luxon said this on 7 Oct 2025, the then-published provisional figure for the July 2025 year was 73,300, about 11% above 2023 and reported everywhere as a record, so he was contradicting the official numbers as they stood. Those provisional estimates were subsequently revised down (AAP's April 2026 fact check found the revised peak was 67,812 in the year to April 2024, not a record), which is what vindicates the claim. A secondary caveat: if 'last year he was PM' is read as the 12 months to Nov 2023 rather than calendar 2023, the base would be somewhat lower because departures were rising through 2023, widening the gap to roughly 5%.

statement: Does he accept that there are 36,000 fewer jobs under his leadership than when he started as Prime Minister?
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / filled jobs series; compare total employment or filled jobs at Nov 2023 with the latest print before Oct 2025; true if the fall is approximately 36,000, false if materially different or if employment rose.
reasoning: Criterion: compare total employment / filled jobs at Nov 2023 (Luxon sworn in 27 Nov 2023) with the latest print before Oct 2025; true if the fall is approximately 36,000. Stats NZ Monthly Employment Indicators: seasonally adjusted filled jobs were about 2.38-2.385 million in Nov 2023 (the Dec 2023 release reported Dec 2023 at 2.39 million, up 4,746 on November), against 2.35 million in Aug 2025 (the last MEI print before the statement, released 29 Sep 2025) — a fall of roughly 35,000, matching the claimed 36,000. The HLFS gives the same picture: employment hit an all-time high of 2,917,000 in the Dec 2023 quarter and was down about 1.2% by mid-2025, i.e. roughly 35,000-37,000 fewer. Independent corroboration: Bloomberg reported filled jobs back at early-2023 levels by mid-2025, and the NZCTU later counted 41,465 fewer filled jobs over the two years to Feb 2026. Employment clearly fell rather than rose, and the magnitude is right. Minor caveat: the Nov 2023 level comes from the 2023-vintage series and MEI figures are routinely revised, so the exact gap carries a few thousand jobs of uncertainty.

statement: As I’ve tried to explain before, when Governments increase spending by 84 percent, that takes inflation up to 7.5 percent and that leads to 12 or 13 interest rate rises, which then puts an economy into recession.
criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses, 2017/18 vs 2022/23 (true if the increase is ~84%); Stats NZ CPI annual peak during 2021-23 (true if ~7.5%, false if materially lower); RBNZ OCR decisions Oct 2021 - May 2023 (true if 12-13 increases).
reasoning: Three checkable components, two of which fail the criterion as written. (1) SPENDING +84%: the criterion specifies Treasury core Crown expenses 2017/18 vs 2022/23. Actuals are $80.6b (year ended 30 June 2018) and $127.6b (year ended 30 June 2023) = +58.3%, materially below 84%. An 84%-ish figure is only reachable by comparing 2016/17 ($76.3b) with 2023/24 ($139.0b) = +82%, a window that includes the current government's own first budget year and so does not support the attribution to the previous government's spending. (2) INFLATION 7.5%: Stats NZ annual CPI peaked at 7.3% in the June 2022 quarter (a 32-year high), not 7.5% — overstated, though only slightly. (3) 12-13 RATE RISES: correct. The RBNZ raised the OCR at 12 consecutive decisions from October 2021 (0.25%) to May 2023 (5.50%), a fact recorded in KPMG's debt market commentary on the May 2023 decision; the criterion's 12-13 band is satisfied. The trailing 'recession' assertion is a causal chain rather than a discrete number and was not part of the criterion; New Zealand did experience contraction over this period. Net: the OCR count is right, the inflation peak is mildly overstated, and the headline 84% spending figure is not supported for the period the speaker attributes it to.

statement: If all of those things were so successful, why is it that capital hospital spending has halved under his leadership, with almost $800 million less being spent on upgrading our hospitals now than when he became Prime Minister?
criterion: Health NZ / Vote Health capital expenditure on hospital infrastructure, 2023/24 baseline vs the latest year; true if the annual figure has roughly halved and the fall is close to $800 million, false if materially smaller or if capital spending rose.
reasoning: The criterion asks for Health NZ / Vote Health capital expenditure on hospital infrastructure, 2023/24 baseline vs the latest year, and tests whether the annual figure roughly halved with a fall close to $800m. I could not retrieve either primary actual: the Health NZ annual reports for 2023/24 and 2024/25 (which hold the audited capital expenditure figures) returned HTTP 403 or exceeded the fetch size limit, and the Ministry of Health and RNZ pages carrying the derived figures also 403'd. What I could verify points to a real decline that is materially smaller than claimed, and one figure points the other way. Budget capital allocations for health fell from $1.3b at Budget 2023 to $1.013b at Budget 2025 — a fall of roughly $290m, about 23%, not a halving and not ~$800m. Separately, Health NZ's 2025/26 Statement of Performance Expectations planned $2.869b of capital expenditure, described as an uplift of $1.326b (85%) above actual capital expenditure delivered in 2024/25, which implies 2024/25 actual capex of roughly $1.54b — inconsistent with a halving to ~$0.8b. The substantive grievance behind the claim is well documented: an official report found Health NZ 'significantly underspending its capital expenditure' against forecast, with a $315m first-quarter 2025/26 gap (including $190m on buildings and plant), and projects stuck in planning. So hospital capital delivery genuinely fell short, but the specific 'halved / almost $800 million less' magnitude is not corroborated by anything I could reach, and the one solid year-on-year datapoint cuts against it. Flagging that a definitive verdict would require the two annual report figures I could not obtain.

statement: Why should New Zealanders believe anything that the Prime Minister has just said when he declared that 2025 was all about “growth, growth, growth”, and what he’s actually delivered is a shrinking economy, with New Zealand now 2.8 percent smaller per capita than when he became Prime Minister?
criterion: Stats NZ real GDP per capita series; compare the Dec 2023 quarter with the June 2025 quarter; true if the cumulative fall is approximately 2.8%, false if materially different.
reasoning: The claim was made on 7 October 2025, so the latest data available was the June 2025 quarter GDP release (18 September 2025), which showed GDP falling 0.9% in the quarter and GDP per capita falling 1.1%. Reporting on that release states GDP per capita fell 2.1% over the past year and 3.9% since the June 2023 quarter. Luxon took office on 27 November 2023, i.e. during the December 2023 quarter, so the natural baselines are the September 2023 quarter (the last full quarter before he became PM) or the December 2023 quarter. Stats NZ recorded GDP per capita falling 0.9% in the September 2023 quarter and 0.7% in the December 2023 quarter. Backing those out of the -3.9% cumulative gives approximately -3.0% measured from the end of the September 2023 quarter and approximately -2.4% measured from the end of the December 2023 quarter. Hipkins' 2.8% sits between the two defensible baselines and is within a few tenths of a percentage point of either. It is not a materially overstated figure, and the direction and rough magnitude — a shrinking per-capita economy under a government campaigning on 'growth' — are correct. Note this is a derivation from published quarterly changes rather than a direct read of the per-capita index, and GDP figures are subject to revision, so the exact decimal is soft; the substance is not.

statement: As I said in the House a couple of weeks ago, forecasters were predicting a negative GDP result for the June quarter; they got a little more than expected: GDP was reported at negative 0.9 percent for the quarter, following positive growth of 0.9 percent in the previous quarter.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP release of 18 September 2025; true if the June 2025 quarter was reported at -0.9% and the March quarter at +0.9%, false if either figure differs.
reasoning: Stats NZ's quarterly GDP release of 18 September 2025 reports the June 2025 quarter at -0.9% (seasonally adjusted), following a revised +0.9% in the March 2025 quarter. Both figures in the quote match the release exactly. The 'more than expected' framing also checks out: market consensus was around -0.3% to -0.4%, and the fall was described as far worse than forecast.

statement: New Zealand has a longstanding “do not travel” advisory in place for Gaza. The advisory explicitly warns New Zealanders that any attempt to enter Gaza by sea is in breach of Israeli Navy restrictions, including participation in flotillas to deliver aid.
criterion: The MFAT SafeTravel advisory for Gaza / the Palestinian Territories as it stood on 7 October 2025 (including archived versions): true if the advisory level is 'do not travel' and its text expressly warns against attempting to enter Gaza by sea and references Israeli naval restrictions or flotillas; false if no such advisory existed, or if the advisory contains no sea-entry/flotilla warning.
reasoning: MFAT's own official page states New Zealand has a longstanding 'do not travel' advisory for Gaza and that 'the advisory explicitly warns New Zealanders against any attempt to enter Gaza by sea in breach of Israeli navy restrictions, including participation in flotillas to deliver aid' - the same sentence Peters used. MFAT's proactively released internal media lines dated 10 and 11 October 2025 (OIA 30542) carry that wording verbatim, confirming it was the ministry's stated position within days of the quote. Disconfirming check: I could not retrieve the SafeTravel advisory text as it stood on 7 October 2025 (Wayback unreachable from this environment; the availability API returns no snapshot for that date), and the current destination page, last updated 25 June 2026, is still 'Do not travel' but no longer contains sea-entry/flotilla wording. So the advisory level and the ministry's characterisation of its content are both confirmed from official sources, but the October 2025 text itself was not directly inspected.

statement: That’s why our energy package tackles the root causes: limited fuel supply, a shortage of back-up generation in dry years, and years of policy uncertainty. The issues add a risk premium of between $240 and $400 annually on Kiwis’ household power bills.
criterion: The Frontier Economics review of the electricity market commissioned by the Government (published 2025) and the accompanying MBIE/Ministerial energy package documents: true if a modelled risk premium in the $240–$400 per household per year range appears there; false if no such figure is produced, or if the source figure is materially different in size or refers to something other than household bills.
reasoning: The underlying premium is real and government-sourced: the Beehive fact sheet released with the October 2025 energy package (drawing on the Frontier Economics review) states that ASX electricity contract prices now include a $30-50/MWh 'risk premium' because of dry-year exposure, and attributes it to the causes Watts named (fuel supply, no dry-year backup generation, policy risk deterring investment). But no $240-$400 per-household figure appears in the Frontier review or the package documents. The published figure applies to wholesale contract prices per MWh, not household bills. $240-$400 is Watts' own conversion at MBIE's 8,000 kWh modelled household; the Government's own later translation of the same premium, given by Energy Minister Simeon Brown in June 2026, is $210-$350 a year for an average household (~7,000 kWh, closer to actual average consumption of ~7,084 kWh). So the substance holds but the household figure is an unpublished extrapolation at the top of the plausible range, roughly 15% above the Government's own per-household number.

statement: How exactly does he reconcile his statement to young people “The world doesn’t owe you a living.” with his $3 billion tax cut to landlords?
criterion: Treasury and Budget costings for the restoration of interest deductibility on residential rental property. True if the forecast revenue foregone over the forecast period is approximately $3 billion; false if the official costing is materially different.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the official costing of restoring interest deductibility on residential rental property is approximately $3 billion over the forecast period. Government data released with the March 2024 announcement costs it at $2.9 billion over the four-year forecast period — up $800m on National's pre-election $2.1b estimate, because the National-ACT coalition agreement accelerated the phase-in (60% in 2023/24, 80% in 2024/25, 100% in 2025/26). $2.9b rounds to the $3b Swarbrick cited. No later revision away from that figure was found; reporting from March 2024 onward consistently uses $2.9b. Caveats that do not change the verdict against the criterion as written: it is revenue foregone over four years rather than an annual cost, and it is a tax change rather than a cash transfer — Swarbrick signalled neither, but did not misstate the magnitude.

statement: How is it fair to scapegoat young people as being “lazy, sitting on the couch playing PlayStation” when there are far more job seekers than jobs in almost every region in the country, and when they are competing for those jobs with people more experienced than they are?
criterion: The public record of Christopher Luxon's remarks (Hansard, press conference transcripts, RNZ/Newsroom reporting) up to 7 October 2025. True if he characterised young jobseekers as lazy or as sitting on the couch playing PlayStation; false if no such remark is on the record.
reasoning: The criterion is disjunctive: true if Luxon characterised young jobseekers as lazy OR as sitting on the couch playing PlayStation. The PlayStation limb is verbatim on the public record and predates 7 October 2025. At the Rotorua Business Chamber's Westpac Smarts luncheon on 3 October 2025 he said of 18- and 19-year-olds out of school: "I'm sorry, we're not paying your benefit... That's your parents' responsibility... You've got to get off the couch, stop playing PlayStation and go find a job." On 5 October, announcing the means-testing of Jobseeker Support for 18-19 year olds, he added "the world doesn't owe you a living and nor, except in limited circumstances, do taxpayers" and framed the benefit as not a "lifestyle choice". Checking for the disconfirming case: he did NOT use the word "lazy" — that is Davidson's gloss, and her quotation marks compress two separate remarks into one. But the criterion's second limb is met exactly. Her surrounding premise (more jobseekers than jobs in almost every region) is also supported: RNZ found just under four unemployed people per job ad nationwide, with more unemployed than vacancies in almost all parts of the country.

statement: Let’s be clear: the Labour-Greens Government had a 3.5 percent unemployment rate and still put 60,000 people on the jobseeker benefit. It’s because they don’t care about young people in New Zealand.
criterion: Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate during the 2017–2023 government and MSD Jobseeker Support recipient numbers over the same period. True if the unemployment rate reached about 3.5% while jobseeker numbers rose by roughly 60,000; false if either figure is materially different.
reasoning: Criterion: true if HLFS unemployment reached about 3.5% during the 2017-2023 government and MSD Jobseeker Support numbers rose by roughly 60,000 over the same period. Both hold. Stats NZ HLFS: seasonally adjusted unemployment was 3.2% in the December 2021 quarter (the lowest since the series began in 1986), 3.3% in June 2022 and 3.4% in December 2022 — so ~3.5% is a fair characterisation. MSD Jobseeker Support: about 120,700 working-age recipients at end-September 2017 (derived from the September 2018 fact sheet, which reports an 8,917 rise to 129,643), versus roughly 183,000-186,000 by late 2023 (Social Development Minister Upston puts it as a 54% rise across Labour's six years; ~190,000 by December 2023, and 204,765 by September 2024 after a further 12% year-on-year jump). That is an increase of roughly 60,000-65,000. Two framings the underlying numbers do not support, though the criterion does not test them: "Labour-Greens Government" overstates the Greens' role (Labour governed alone with a single-party majority from 2020), and the two figures are not simultaneous — the bulk of the jobseeker increase came in the 2020 COVID year, whereas the 3.2-3.4% unemployment prints came in 2021-22 while jobseeker numbers were falling back from their ~2021 peak. The causal "put 60,000 people on the benefit" is therefore rhetoric layered on two individually accurate figures.

statement: The report specifically cited the ban on offshore exploration, the 100 percent renewable target, and Lake Onslow as to why we are short on investment in fuel and firming, and that has left us dangerously short of reliable back-up generation.
criterion: The text of the Frontier Economics electricity market report: true if it names all three of those policies as causes of reduced investment in fuel and firming; false if it names none, or attributes the shortfall to other causes without citing them.
reasoning: Frontier's headline finding supports the second half of the claim: the Beehive fact sheet states the Government agrees with 'Frontier's key finding: the market will not currently deliver investment in the dry-year backup supplies that New Zealand requires, and so intervention is required.' Frontier's core diagnosis is that 'the policy risk and preferences of shareholders mean that there is a disincentive to invest in the thermal assets needed to support dry year risk', and that government policy volatility means 'at the stroke of a pen the value of an investment can be destroyed.' Contemporaneous reporting on the released report (Newsroom, RNZ, Heft) says Frontier pointed to the offshore exploration ban, the 100 per cent renewable target and Lake Onslow/NZ Battery as examples of the policy shifts that eroded investor confidence, so all three do appear as cited causes. However, Watts overstates the report's framing in two ways. First, Frontier does not present those three policies as the explanation for the firming shortfall; it lists them as illustrations of policy risk alongside other causes it treats as at least as important — the investment preferences of the Crown-majority MOM shareholders, falling thermal utilisation as renewables grow, highly uncertain dry-year revenue, expectations of government intervention ('soft price caps'), and high upfront costs (Simpson Grierson's summary of the review cites only 'high upfront costs, uncertain returns, and policy risks'). Second, 'dangerously short of reliable back-up generation' is Watts's characterisation; the same report found the market 'is performing well in delivering a strong pipeline of cheaper renewable generation.' Caveat on method: MBIE blocks automated retrieval of the report PDF, so I verified the three-policy attribution through the Beehive fact sheet and secondary reporting rather than the report text itself.

statement: Does he take responsibility for the 36,000 fewer jobs and 10,000 more unemployed young people since he came into office and implemented his economic policies?
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / filled-jobs series and the 15–24 unemployment count, comparing the quarter before the government took office (Q3 2023) with the most recent 2025 quarter. True if employment is roughly 36,000 lower and youth unemployed roughly 10,000 higher; false if either movement is materially different or of the opposite sign.
reasoning: Checked against the criterion's specified comparison: Q3 2023 (the quarter before the government took office) versus the most recent quarter available when she spoke on 7 October 2025, which is the June 2025 quarter (released 6 August 2025; the September 2025 quarter was not published until November). Seasonally adjusted HLFS employment (OECD/Stats NZ series via FRED) was 2,907,000 in 2023Q3 and 2,872,000 in 2025Q2 — 35,000 lower, which rounds to her 36,000 within the series' 1,000-person rounding. The direction and magnitude are confirmed. Youth: the number of unemployed 15-24 year olds rose from 52,544 (2023Q3) to 66,939 (2025Q2), an increase of about 14,400, with the 15-24 unemployment rate going from 11.7% to 15.4% on a shrinking youth labour force (450,400 to 433,900). So the youth movement is in the direction she claimed and is in fact larger than the 10,000 she cited — she understated it rather than overstating it. Disconfirming check: no quarter in the window shows employment above the 2023Q3 level or youth unemployment below it, so neither movement has the opposite sign. Note the claim is about the numbers only; whether the government's policies caused these movements is a separate question this verdict does not address.

statement: This is a Government that is actually making sure the mess that was Te Pūkenga—the $300 million that was wasted—the polytechnics are put back into regional New Zealand to connect people with work.
criterion: Te Pūkenga annual reports and Tertiary Education Commission / Ministry of Education figures on merger costs and accumulated deficits. True if approximately $300 million is identifiable as expenditure or losses attributable to the Te Pūkenga merger; false if the documented figure is materially smaller or cannot be attributed to the merger.
reasoning: No single documented figure of '$300 million wasted' on the Te Pukenga merger exists in the annual reports or TEC/Ministry material. What is documented: Te Pukenga received $121 million in Crown funding for establishment and transition to the end of 2022; National (Penny Simmonds) counted roughly $200 million spent on the merger by 2023, including $120m of merger spending and 149 additional head-office positions as at 2022; the consolidated operating deficit was about $80 million in 2022 and $37.9 million in 2023 (reduced from a forecast $93.4m, and a $35.6m surplus once land and building revaluations are counted); 2024 produced a $16.6 million surplus. Adding establishment/merger spend to the 2022-23 operating deficits gets to roughly $240-320 million, so a figure 'approximately $300 million' is reachable, but only by bundling appropriated merger funding with operating deficits. The attribution to the merger is contested on the record: the ITP sector already ran a $48 million deficit in 2019 before the reforms, and Te Pukenga argued the 16 polytechnics would have lost about $280 million over the same period without the merger. Disconfirming evidence checked: the nearest hard '$300m' numbers in the record are not merger costs at all - Te Pukenga's 2023 Budget bid of $330 million (mostly IT, largely not granted), the $423 million business case for full integration, and RNZ's August 2024 finding that the Government's own preferred disestablishment option could produce losses of $297 million over four years. So the order of magnitude is defensible but the specific '$300 million that was wasted' is a rounded political aggregate, not an identifiable documented figure attributable to the merger.

statement: How does New Zealand’s road to economic recovery in the June 2025 quarter, that saw a contraction of 0.9 percent, compare to Canada’s, who are more directly affected by US tariffs?
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP release for the June 2025 quarter. True if real GDP contracted by approximately 0.9%; false if the published figure is materially different.
reasoning: Stats NZ's Gross domestic product: June 2025 quarter release (18 September 2025) reports that real GDP decreased 0.9 percent in the June 2025 quarter (seasonally adjusted, production measure), driven by manufacturing (-3.5%) and construction (-1.8%), with falls in 10 of 16 industries. This matches the cited figure exactly. Disconfirming check: the result was worse than the ~0.3-0.4% contraction economists and the RBNZ had forecast, so a smaller published figure was the plausible alternative and it did not occur. Per capita GDP fell 1.1%.

statement: Well, these comparisons are interesting; however, I note that the member did not make those comparisons in the first quarter of the year when New Zealand’s growth rate was three times the rate of Australia’s.
criterion: Stats NZ and Australian Bureau of Statistics quarterly real GDP growth for the March 2025 quarter. True if New Zealand's quarterly growth rate was approximately three times Australia's; false if materially different.
reasoning: On the data available when Willis spoke (7 Oct 2025): Stats NZ's June-quarter release (18 Sep 2025) revised the March 2025 quarter up to +0.9% (originally published 19 Jun 2025 as +0.8%). The ABS June-quarter national accounts (3 Sep 2025) revised Australia's March 2025 quarter up by 0.1pp to +0.3% (originally +0.2%). 0.9 / 0.3 = exactly three times, so the claim holds on the current vintage. Disconfirming check: on the original vintages the ratio was 0.8/0.2 = four times, i.e. the alternative reading makes NZ's outperformance larger, not smaller, so the claim is not overstated under either vintage. Annual-growth readings would not support 'three times' but the speaker's context is the quarterly comparison.

statement: I’d also note that the same commentary which the member is selectively quoting from now implores the Opposition to do a much better job and notes that they pose a significant risk to the future of the New Zealand economy.
criterion: The 2025 business-leader commentary (Mood of the Boardroom) from which the questioner's quote is drawn. True if the same document urges the Opposition to do better and describes it as a significant risk to the economy; false if it contains no such passage.
reasoning: Half the claim is confirmed, half is not. CONFIRMED: Mood of the Boardroom 2025 (survey run 15 Aug-12 Sep 2025, 150 respondents) does urge the Opposition to do much better. Hipkins scored 2.01/5 on holding the Government to account, with more than 70% giving him 1 or 2 out of 5; Labour's front bench scored poorly overall; CEOs are quoted saying 'The Opposition should be holding the Government to account but right now they feel missing in action... where the bloody hell are ya?', 'We need a stronger opposition and option - and fast!', and 'New Zealand deserves an opposition that is keeping things competitive' (Simon Bridges). NOT CONFIRMED: no passage found in which the survey notes that the Opposition poses a significant risk to the future of the New Zealand economy. The risks MOTB 2025 identifies for the economy are US tariffs, geopolitical deterioration and the erosion of multilateral trade rules, China's weakness, and subdued consumer confidence; a change of government is not among them, and overall economy confidence fell to 2.81/5 for those reasons. Disconfirming search for the opposite framing surfaced only scattered respondent unease about a hypothetical Labour-Greens-Te Pati Maori arrangement handing influence to 'more activist policy positions' (one chair: 'the completely looney tune of Labour with the very left Greens and radical Maori party') - individual anxiety about a possible future coalition, not a survey finding that the Opposition is a significant economic risk. So the substance is materially overstated in its second clause. Limitation: parliament.nz served a bot-protection page, so I could not retrieve the 7 October 2025 Hansard to independently confirm that the commentary Edmonds quoted was Mood of the Boardroom; I judged against MOTB as the criterion specifies. Herald articles are partly paywalled and were read via page fetch.

statement: Who else does she blame for 36,000 fewer jobs, 2,700 company liquidations, the 200 Kiwis who leave every day, and a shrinking economy, given the Government has blamed the previous Government, US tariffs, merchants of misery, teenagers, and even John Key?
criterion: Stats NZ HLFS employment change over the government's term, Companies Office / NZ liquidation statistics for the year to late 2025, and Stats NZ international migration departures. True if employment is down about 36,000, liquidations number about 2,700 in the period referenced, and net departures average about 200 a day; false if any of the three is materially wrong.
reasoning: All three named checks hold, plus the 'shrinking economy' rider. JOBS: Stats NZ HLFS put seasonally adjusted employment at 2,939,000 in the Dec 2023 quarter (the quarter Luxon took office) and 2,882,000 in the June 2025 quarter — the latest data available on 7 Oct 2025 — a fall of ~57,000; on the monthly filled-jobs (MEI) series, Aug 2025 was down 17,442 (0.7%) year-on-year at 2.33m actual / 2.35m seasonally adjusted, roughly 40,000 below the late-2023 level. Either series makes '36,000 fewer jobs' correct in magnitude and, if anything, understated; the same figure was Labour's standard line that week (Hipkins: 'There are 36,000 fewer jobs today than there were when Christopher Luxon became Prime Minister'). I could not pin the exact series that yields precisely 36,000 (likely the rebased HLFS vintage), but no plausible series makes it an overstatement. LIQUIDATIONS: calendar 2025 finished at 2,867 reported liquidations, a 15-year high and +13.5% on 2024 (~2,526); Centrix recorded 306 in September 2025 alone, the highest month in a decade. A rolling 12 months to ~Sept 2025 therefore lands around 2,700–2,800, so '2,700' is accurate for the period she could cite. DEPARTURES: Stats NZ recorded 72,700 migrant departures of NZ citizens in the September 2025 year (73,900 in the August 2025 year, the record) — 199 and 202 a day respectively, an essentially exact match for '200 Kiwis who leave every day' as spoken. Note the criterion says 'net departures ~200 a day'; on a net basis the loss was 46,400 (127/day), so the claim is true on gross departures — which is what 'Kiwis who leave' means — not on net. SHRINKING ECONOMY: GDP fell 0.9% in the June 2025 quarter (released 18 Sept 2025), the sharpest of three falls in five quarters. Disconfirming check: I looked for a Stats NZ series showing employment up over the term and for a liquidation count materially below 2,700 for a year ending in 2025 — neither exists. Incidentally the rhetorical list is also grounded: Nicola Willis publicly blamed the US tariff rollout for the June-quarter GDP fall.

statement: The current system has the best of intentions but has placed a heavy financial burden on property owners, leaving 5,800 buildings currently still awaiting either remediation or demolition.
criterion: MBIE's EPB register / national earthquake-prone building statistics as at October 2025; true if the count of buildings still awaiting remediation or demolition is approximately 5,800, false if materially different (e.g. under 4,000 or over 8,000).
reasoning: The figure matches the official count in circulation at the time, and is inside the criterion's band. When the Government announced the earthquake-prone building overhaul on 29 September 2025, 1News reported — on figures supplied by Building and Construction Minister Chris Penk's own office — that 'Around 5800 buildings on the register are currently awaiting remediation or demolition under the existing system which has overall seen more than 8000 structures classed.' Penk's 7 October statement repeats that number. Disconfirming check: an independent analysis by Sapere (published 7 Oct 2025) working from the MBIE EPB register as at January 2025 counts 6,717 unique buildings ever listed, of which ~1,714 are no longer earthquake-prone (945 strengthened, 258 demolished, 361 reassessed), leaving 'over 5,000' still on the register — i.e. ~5,000 rather than 5,800, because it uses the narrower 'ever listed' base of 6,717 rather than the 8,000+ 'classed' base. The Government's own review documents imply a working base of ~5,300 (55% removed ≈ 2,900, plus 1,440 cheaper remediation + 840 no work + ~80 full retrofit). So credible counts span roughly 5,000–5,800 depending on the base used; the criterion fails the claim only below 4,000 or above 8,000, and none of the counts come close to those bounds. The claim is true, with the caveat that 5,800 sits at the top of the credible range.

statement: Out in the real world, Tararua District Mayor Tracy Collis says that the changes indicate the survival of rural New Zealand.
criterion: Public statements, media releases or news reports from Tararua District Mayor Tracy Collis in the week to 7 October 2025; true if she publicly characterised the changes in these terms, false if no such statement exists or she said something materially different.
reasoning: The statement exists, is from the named person in the named role, and is quoted almost verbatim. The Post published an article on 29 September 2025 headlined 'New earthquake regulations ensure "survival of rural New Zealand"', reporting Tararua District Mayor Tracey Collis's reaction to MBIE's announced changes to the earthquake-prone building rules; her words were 'It really does indicate the survival of rural New Zealand.' Penk's rendering — 'says that the changes indicate the survival of rural New Zealand' — reproduces her verb ('indicate') and phrase exactly. Corroborating context: Tararua District Council issued a release in September 2025 welcoming the review, noting the district has 107 buildings listed as earthquake-prone, many heritage, and that lower strengthening costs 'will come as real relief'; Collis separately said the council had been lobbying for the change 'over two Governments'. The change specifically exempts unreinforced masonry buildings under three storeys in towns under 10,000 people, which is why a rural mayor framed it in survival terms. Disconfirming check: I looked for other mayors who might be the real source of the phrase — Andy Watson (Rangitīkei), Susan O'Regan (Waipā), Max Baxter (Ōtorohanga) and John Robertson (Waitomo) all commented on the reform in the same period, but none used this phrasing, and the article carrying it is about Tararua. The only discrepancy is the spelling of her first name: it is Tracey, not Tracy — a Hansard transcription artefact, not a factual error.

statement: What costs has New Zealand incurred in the nine years since the earthquake-prone building rules came into place, and was ACT right, in hindsight, to be the only party opposed to the 2016 bill?
criterion: The division record for the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill's third reading in 2016; true if ACT was the sole party recorded against, false if it voted for it or if any other party also voted against.
reasoning: The criterion asks for the third reading division of the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill 2016: true if ACT was the sole party recorded against. Parliament's Hansard pages (51HansD_20160510_00000024) are behind Radware bot protection and could not be fetched, so the division record itself was unreachable. Secondary evidence is consistent and uncontradicted: ACT's own release states 'I voted 1 against 120 to oppose this law', and RNZ reports Seymour 'was the lone MP in 2016 who stood against the Earthquake-prone Buildings law'. A 120-1 party vote leaves no room for any other party to have voted Noe, and legal commentary (Buddle Findlay, ATC) describes the amended bill as having attracted cross-party support, which fits. Disconfirming check: no source found reporting the Greens, Maori Party, NZ First or any other party voting against at third reading; the RNZ report about Greens opposing at first reading concerns the separate 2025 bill. Caveat on sourcing: the vote count originates with Seymour himself, relayed by RNZ, rather than from the primary division record. (Luxton's framing of 'nine years since the rules came into place' is loose - assent May 2016, provisions in force 1 July 2017 - but the criterion does not test that.)

statement: There are 19 marine protection areas that have been created and there is further investment of putea, time, effort, and energy that will be announced in short course.
criterion: The text of the Hauraki Gulf Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill as reported back from select committee, and the accompanying Department of Conservation / Ministry for the Environment material; true if the number of marine protection areas established or extended by the bill is 19, false if the count is materially different.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the number of marine protection areas established or extended by the Hauraki Gulf Tikapa Moana Marine Protection Bill is 19, per DOC/MfE material. DOC's Revitalising the Gulf page gives exactly 19, broken down as 2 marine reserve extensions (Cape Rodney-Okakari Point / Goat Island and Te Whanganui-o-Hei / Cathedral Cove), 12 high protection areas, and 5 seafloor protection areas - '19 new protection zones', described as the most significant increase in marine protection in over a decade. Independent coverage (Greenpeace Aotearoa, Mountains to Sea, Oceanographic) reports the same 12 + 5 + 2 structure, so the count is not a DOC-only framing. The Act came into effect 25 October 2025, shortly after the 7 October statement. Only slack: Potaka said 'created', and 2 of the 19 are extensions of existing reserves rather than newly created areas - but the criterion explicitly covers 'established or extended', so this does not reduce the verdict. Disconfirming check: no source found giving a materially different count (e.g. 17 or 21) for the bill as reported back or as passed; the late select-committee change was a fishing exemption, not a change in the number of areas.

statement: Well, at just over 5 percent, our unemployment rate is actually below what it has been, on average, over the last 15 years or so.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate for the quarter current at 7 October 2025, compared with the arithmetic mean of the quarterly HLFS unemployment rate over the 15 years to that date. True if the current rate is at or just above 5% AND is lower than that 15-year mean; false if the current rate is materially different from 'just over 5 percent' or is at or above the 15-year mean.
reasoning: The criterion requires both that the current rate be at or just above 5% AND lower than the 15-year mean of quarterly HLFS rates. The first half holds, the second fails. At 7 October 2025 the current HLFS quarter was June 2025, seasonally adjusted unemployment 5.2% (Stats NZ) - fairly described as 'just over 5 percent'. Taking the 60 quarterly HLFS observations from the September 2010 quarter through the June 2025 quarter (OECD/FRED series LRUNTTTTNZQ156S, sourced from Stats NZ HLFS; the 2025-04-01 observation of 5.2 matches the Stats NZ June 2025 release, confirming alignment), the arithmetic mean is 293.9/60 = 4.90%. The current 5.2% is therefore roughly 0.3 percentage points ABOVE the 15-year average, not below it - the criterion's explicit falsifying condition. Disconfirming check: I tested whether a looser reading of 'the last 15 years or so' rescues the claim. Extending the window back to the GFC (2008 Q1, ~17.5 years) only lifts the mean to ~4.97%; pre-2008 quarters were around 3.7-4%, so pushing the window further back lowers the mean rather than raising it. No plausible start date within or near '15 years or so' produces a mean at or above 5.2%.

statement: What evidence does he have that whānau earning just over $65,000 a year can afford to support an 18- or 19-year-old, when two parents on minimum wage already exceed that threshold by $33,000, with no allowance for rent, other tamariki, or the rising cost of living?
criterion: The NZ adult minimum wage in force on 7 October 2025, multiplied by two full-time (40-hour) earners over 52 weeks, compared with the stated parental income threshold of $65,529. True if the excess is approximately $33,000 (within a few thousand dollars); false if the excess is materially different.
reasoning: The NZ adult minimum wage in force on 7 October 2025 was $23.50/hour (Minimum Wage Order 2025, effective 1 April 2025; the $23.95 rate only took effect 1 April 2026). Two full-time earners at 40 hours x 52 weeks = $48,880 each, $97,760 combined. The Parental Assistance Test income limit is confirmed at $65,529, giving an excess of $32,231; against the '$65,000' figure she said aloud, $32,760. Both are within ~$800 of her stated $33,000, well inside the criterion's 'few thousand dollars' tolerance. Checked for disconfirmation: no lower minimum wage rate applied on that date (the starting-out/training rate of $18.80 would not apply to two adult parents), and no alternative official threshold exists.

statement: What measures, if any, will the Prime Minister put in place to stop the 4,300 young people expected to lose jobseeker support next year from falling into poverty, homelessness, or leaving Aotearoa entirely?
criterion: MSD advice, the Regulatory Impact Statement, or Ministerial announcements for the Parental Assistance Test / youth jobseeker changes, for the projected number of young people losing jobseeker support in 2026. True if the official projection is approximately 4,300; false if the published projection is materially different or no such projection exists.
reasoning: The Government announced the Parental Assistance Test on 5 October 2025 (two days before the quote), with an official estimate that of the 15,045 18- and 19-year-olds currently on Jobseeker Support, approximately 4,300 would become ineligible (and about 4,700 would remain eligible). The start date was brought forward to November 2026, so 'next year' is correct relative to a 7 October 2025 speech. Disconfirming check: the earlier Budget 2025 MSD factsheet gives different figures (~17,800 not eligible over the first two years, from July 2027), but that is the superseded pre-announcement design; the October 2025 announcement is the operative advice and matches 4,300.

statement: Evidence shows us that if a young person goes on to welfare before the age of 25, they can spend, on average, another 18 years on benefit over their lifetime.
criterion: The MSD benefit system actuarial valuation (Taylor Fry) figures for average future years on benefit for clients entering the system under age 25. True if the published average is approximately 18 years; false if the published figure is materially different or measures something other than lifetime years on benefit.
reasoning: MSD's published 'Future years on benefit' figures, from the Taylor Fry Social Outcomes Model (September 2022 modelling, released under the OIA), give an average of 18.9 future years on a main benefit for Jobseeker Support clients aged under 25, and 21.3 years for all under-25 main benefit clients. MSD and Ministers state under-25 Jobseeker clients 'would spend an average of about 18 more years on a benefit over their lifetimes'. The metric is explicitly average future years on a main benefit over the person's remaining lifetime (not necessarily continuous), which is what Upston described as 'another 18 years on benefit over their lifetime' - so the criterion's disqualifier (measuring something other than lifetime years on benefit) does not apply. If anything 18 is the conservative end of the published range.

statement: How many construction jobs were lost when the Government cancelled 3,500 Kāinga Ora homes?
criterion: Kāinga Ora build programme documents, Budget 2024/2025 papers, or Ministerial announcements recording the number of planned Kāinga Ora homes stopped or removed from the programme. True if approximately 3,500 planned homes were cancelled or descoped; false if the number is materially different or the homes were never funded/committed.
reasoning: Confirmed against the criterion. On 19 June 2025 Kāinga Ora announced that 212 planned projects comprising approximately 3,479 homes would not proceed, following the second stage of assessments under the Government's turnaround plan. The Spinoff reported the same figures ('212 planned housing projects totalling nearly 3,500 state homes'), with $190–220m of already-spent scoping and planning costs written down; RNZ and the Labour Party release use the same ~3,500 number. These were committed, funded programme projects at scoping/early-delivery stage — $190–220m had already been spent on them — so the criterion's failure condition ('never funded/committed') does not apply. One nuance short of falsifying: the decision was formally made by Kāinga Ora's board/CEO and endorsed by Housing Minister Chris Bishop under the Government-directed reset, rather than announced by the Government directly. The number itself, which is what the criterion tests, is accurate to within ~1%.

statement: Does she accept that cutting almost $1 billion of Kāinga Ora’s building spend has contributed to the 20,000 jobs lost in the construction sector; if not, why not?
criterion: Budget appropriations for Kāinga Ora capital/building programmes before and after the 2024 and 2025 Budgets, and Stats NZ employment data (HLFS or filled jobs) for the construction sector between 2023 and the September 2025 quarter. True if the reduction approaches $1 billion AND construction employment has fallen by roughly 20,000; false if either figure is materially overstated.
reasoning: The direction of both claims holds, but each number is overstated as at the date of speaking (7 Oct 2025). JOBS: the most recent Stats NZ data available then showed construction employment of 310,000 (seasonally adjusted, June 2023) falling to 294,000 (June 2025) — a loss of 16,000, not 20,000, and reported as such by the NZ Herald in August 2025. The September 2025 quarter subsequently recorded a further 4.5% / 8,982 fall in construction employment, which would carry the cumulative decline past 20,000 — but Stats NZ released that on 5 November 2025, a month after the claim was made, so it cannot retrospectively justify the figure. The NZCTU, using Stats NZ data, put the loss at 19,300 'since the election' as late as March 2026. SPENDING: I could not substantiate a reduction approaching $1 billion in Kāinga Ora's BUILDING spend specifically. Labour's own accounting attributes $435m to the house build programme and 'over $1 billion' to the maintenance fund ($1.5bn combined); Budget 2025 cut $125m of capital from large-scale projects ($1.1bn to $925.6m); the February 2025 turnaround plan cuts debt by $1.8bn and caps builds at ~1,500–2,000 per year against a prior net increase of 3,600 in the year to June 2024. So there are real, large cuts, but the '$1 billion of building spend' framing appears to import the maintenance cut. Under a strict reading of the criterion ('false if either figure is materially overstated') this would fail; partly_true is the more informative verdict because the underlying substance — a large Kāinga Ora building cut and a large construction employment fall — is real and the causal direction is supported by contemporaneous reporting.

statement: Was Kāinga Ora wrong when they advised that $1 billion of building spend supports approximately 5,200 Kiwi jobs?
criterion: Kāinga Ora briefings or advice released under the OIA containing a jobs-per-billion estimate for building spend. True if such advice states approximately 5,200 jobs per $1 billion; false if no such advice exists or it gives a materially different figure.
reasoning: The criterion requires locating Kāinga Ora briefings or OIA-released advice containing a jobs-per-billion estimate for building spend. I searched Kāinga Ora's OIA and proactive-release index, its briefings to incoming ministers (2016/2019/2023), the 2024 Independent Review and Cabinet response papers, HUD and Treasury Budget material, and general web/news for the figure '5,200 jobs' in any Kāinga Ora or NZ construction context. No document containing that figure surfaced.
